The primary goal was to verify the accuracy of existing approximation methods used in computing linearized dynamics, particularly in relation to first-order relativistic theory. We examined both radiation-type equilibrium conditions and standard perfect fluid dynamics. Notably, we discovered that certain approximation methods yield the correct dynamics for both scenarios, and in the case of viscosity we further discovered that they are precision relies on the relationship between viscosity and radius of curvature being much smaller than it needs to be.

Discovering anomalies within large-scale quantum systems is a major challenge due to their intertwined nature and covert behaviors. Traditional quantum measurement anomaly detection methods struggle to cope with significant trends or latent anomalies hidden within the data. Introducing a new approach called InQMAD, a gradual quantum measurement anomaly identification method that effectively identifies anomalies from mild to intense categories without prior knowledge. Inception quantization analysis and measurement-oriented anomaly reconstruction form the core of InQMad, working in unison to extract robust features and preserve quantitative structure from noisy quantum measurements. Furthermore, InQMAD demonstrates superior performance in detecting anomalies across synthetic and real-world quantum data by comparing it to other advanced anomaly detection methods.

Measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution has shown greater potential compared to its non-measurement device independent counterpart, allowing parties to safely share random data with a positive outcome even when utilizing a faulty or malicious measurement device. Recently, a new application, the measurement-device-independent quantum key exchange, was introduced which enables three measurement device-independent parties to individually privately share random data with each other. In this work, a universal simulation framework has been proposed for the measurement-device-independent three-user scenario and the application of this framework is demonstrated for the measurement-device-independent quantum key exchange scenario. Analytical results from this framework provide a means to verify and validate the security of these cryptographic protocols by simulating various measurement devices and random data sources, and have the added benefit of significantly reducing the amount of required security testing from thousands of random data blocks to just a single mock measurement device with no impact on the protocol's security.

We develop a constant-factor approximation algorithm for solving multiple weighted constraint satisfaction problems under general penalty structures. Additionally, we present a PTAS for a particular high-sparsity weighted 3-CUT instance, assuming each edge has a significantly large weight.

This study presents a novel, non-structural, high-order time-discretization technique for solving time-dependent parabolic PDEs and time-dependent average field games within the mean-limits model. We apply the method to a specific class of time-dependent equations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ that include constant-coefficient linear Fokker-Planck equations, constant average field games, and time-dependent Hamilton-Jacobi equations as special cases. For dimension $d\le 3$, numerical experiments suggest the method converges at a second-order rate for constant average field games.

Within the $U_1$ leptoquark model, we analyze lepton universality violations in $B$ decays, 
specifically $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ and $B \to K^{(*)} \mu^+ \mu^-$. 
To understand $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ better, we calculate relevant form factors using QCD light-front sum rules and extract branching ratios and differential decay rates for various values of hadronic momentum transfer, $t$. 
By mapping out the leptoquark parameter space that is consistent with experimental data on $B \to K^{(*)} \mu^+ \mu^-$, 
we identify allowed regions for $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ predictions. 
Our findings suggest $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ will experience significant suppression 
when compared to previous $\bar{B} \to p \bar{\nu} \tau^-$ predictions. 
Additionally, we explore the impact of $\Lambda_b \to p \tau \bar{\nu}$ data on the leptoquark parameter space 
and locate two distinct, $\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})$, viable regions.

This tutorial focuses on utilizing comparisons, visualizations, and explanations of deep neural networks (DNNs) to improve their reliability and robustness.
To make the DNNs' comprehension easier, we recommend employing pre-trained networks and visual tools that break down their internal operations.
Specifically, we discuss various visualizations, such as Grad-CaMap, LIME, and partial dependence plots, that can reveal the inner workings of DNNs.
Furthermore, we explore the role of explanations in improving the reliability and robustness of DNNs, such as employing auto-perturbations to validate their predictions.
This study serves as a resource for researchers using deep learning, and may motivate them to investigate alternative approaches to validating and improving their models.

Astronomers observe that up to one-third of young stars have already lost their magnetic fields by accreting planets, yet the angular momentum should have been retained. This fraction is also believed to be responsible for the rapid spins and creation of jets seen in young stars. Our simulations show that the ingestion of spinning planets can actually strip a star's magnetic field due to the transfer of angular momentum across the star-planet orbit. This field loss contributes to the observed excessive spin of young stars. We estimate that the star-planet interaction-driven loss of a star's magnetic field may strip about one-third of its field, leading to the seen range in the distribution. This holds true for an wide range of masses and temperatures of stars, as well as the observed statistics of surface temperatures of stars. This concludes that the star-planet interaction-driven ingestion of spinning planets can strip a star's magnetic field, contributing to the angular momentum that shapes its spin. This contributes to the seen distribution of the correlation of the stellar surface temperature and stellar rotation rate. This implies that up to one-third of surface temperatures of stars can actually be attributed to the loss of their magnetic fields due to interacting with spinning planets, effectively contributing to the angular momentum that dictates their rapid rotation and spinning.

The surge in deep fake technology has brought forth significant challenges, especially in detecting fabricated news due to its potential to deceive the human eye.
Despite advances in multimodal detection methods, models powered by eye-friendly features still struggle to reach satisfactory performance levels.
We hypothesize that the human tendency to dismiss seemingly plausible but false information can be leveraged to improve the understanding of how news spreads.
We introduce Meta-FactCheck, a novel meta-learning framework that automatically creates false news by combining unrelated audio and video content, without needing real fake news examples.
This allows us to train detectors capable of accurately identifying false news based on both visual and auditory evidence.
Our experiments show that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art false news detection models on three benchmark datasets.

This article delves into the domestic water supply system's water transport issues, 
particularly those arising from periodic flow changes. We provide a theoretical
analysis of flow fluctuations and their impact on pressure variations, incorporating
periodic flow rate patterns in our calculations. The flow rate at a given point is 
derived using both linear and non-linear terms, accounting for the rate at which 
a wave propagates through the pipeline. Numerical simulations are utilized to 
solve the modified equation, which reveals additional speed changes in the pipeline 
due to the interaction of the flow rate and its derivative, resulting in a complex 
velocity field with possible spiral trajectories. We also derive the term for 
acoustic pressure in the pipeline, which originates from the interaction of flow 
rate patterns and wave speed, and can be heard as a mix of frequencies in the 
pipeline.

In systems like financial information or traffic updates, the decision to update status depends on both time and the accumulated number of unprocessed inputs. We examine a discrete-time model where a single server decides to update the status based on these two factors, processing one input at regular intervals or upon sufficient unprocessed inputs accumulating, with the system's capacity being limited. This model, featuring mutual exclusivity and dependency between the factors, poses a complex classification challenge. Although several potential states could represent the system, up to 1 state out of potentially infinite possibilities is accessible. We however, manage to identify and define the accessible state, alongside its corresponding initiation time.

This study introduces three distinct types of quasi-bialgebras derived from set-theoretic solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation, a type of non-linear quasi-bialgebra with an associative multiplication, a non-associative co-multiplication, and a non-associative unit, as well as a solution $B$ to the Yang-Baxter equation, and then provides concrete examples for solvable lattice gases and the quantum harmonic oscillator.

A type of code known as Golay complementary sets (GCS) of complex numbers has historically been primarily studied. However, our research focuses on creating GCS within a set of vectors that change in multiple phases. Utilizing the method of constructing sequences via their periodic auto-correlation profiles, our approach achieves three distinct sizes or lengths for these multi-phase GCS through orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing techniques. Moreover, our method of construction could potentially contribute to the solution of an open question posed by Yang and Wu regarding the existence of certain symmetrical codes. Additionally, our proposed constructions may offer novel applications in radar technology and communications systems, particularly in detecting multiple targets simultaneously through multi-channel matching filter banks.

Quantum effects, arising from an atom's s-state nature, are vital in non-adiabatic electron transfer between valence and conduction bands. We investigate an atom (s-state) situated between two silicon dimer (valley) states and discover that the electron transfer rate is influenced by both the atom and the relative phase of the valley states. A central atom can mediate coupling between distinct valley states, resulting in an interference effect in the electron transfer process that leads to a variation in transfer rates by a factor of three. Moreover, this process is very sensitive to small changes in the position of the atom, allowing for spatial resolution beyond the Bohr radius at a rate of angstrom$^{-1}$. These findings are anticipated to be可利用 for engineering atomic scale devices that exploit silicon's valley degree of freedom.

Graph-structured systems play a crucial role in various applications and are fundamental to understanding the dynamics of many others. With increasing complexity, these systems have become integral to nearly every aspect of human life. However, analyzing and predicting their behavior pose significant challenges due to their intricate nature. Neural network approaches, particularly Graph Neural Networks, have shown promise in processing and analyzing graph-structured data by integrating features from nodes and edges. By aggregating information and establishing connections, these networks have a framework that is well-suited for examining the dynamic relationships within these systems. This paper provides an overview of Graph-structured systems, explores their real-world applications and research challenges, and highlights recent advancements in using Graph- Neural Networks to analyze dynamic relationships within these systems. We also outline a potential framework for studying graph-structured systems through the lens of dynamic networks.

This study introduces a concept called topological division, offering a novel perspective on phenomena observed within homotopy theory, including a potential explanation for the unexpected growth of torsion within stable homotopy groups as dimensional increase. Topological division is defined through the property of a map between spatial entities of equal dimension, where its domain is split into two distinct parts of lower dimension. We establish a formula for calculating the minimal dimensional requirement for such a division to exist, involving scalar values and determining specific conditions under which topological divisions of various types and dimensions can be realized.

Accidental or intentional cerebral lesions cause a wide range of difficulties in clinical practice and clinical research. To study and recreate damage to the brain, computer-aided lesion generation is an essential tool that can produce synthetic lesions to complement experimental data collection. This paper presents a novel cerebral lesion generation framework called Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVE). PAVER creates realistic lesions in healthy brain images by initially generating a low-dimensional latent space representation of the lesion and then using a mask-based segmentation approach to translate this representation into a three-dimensional lesion model. A key innovation of PAVE is its ability to progress from simple to complex lesion forms, ensuring the stability and efficiency of the model. When compared to existing methods, our results indicate that PAVE outperforms competitors in terms of accuracy and efficiency in replicating actual lesion data.

The striking phenomenon of quantum nonlocality, which outperforms classical local hidden variable theories, has significant implications for quantum information processing. To enhance its practical use, it is crucial to develop quantum states that are resistant to environmental disturbances and experimental inaccuracies. In this study, we identify and analyze nonlocality exhibiting robustness in unextendible product states within the context of heterogeneous systems composed of multiple different quantum states. Our findings demonstrate that robust nonlocal correlations persist even for states possessing high fidelity with the unextendible product states, and in some cases, quantum robust Minkowski inequalities have shown nonlocality robustness in these systems. Moreover, we provide evidence that the nonlocality observed in our analysis surpasses the boundaries set by local hidden variable theories.

The Total Secure Coordination (TSC) algorithm is designed to manage the complex task of coordinating multiple autonomous robots working together. One of the key features of this algorithm is its robustness to coordination failures among the robots. We tested the algorithm's effectiveness and safety by using a team of approximately 10 astrobots to collect data for the fifth release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Over the course of more than 700 days of data collection, the astrobots successfully completed this task despite occasional coordination failures. Our results indicate that the TSC algorithm not only performs well but also provides a positive return on investment. Additionally, our research indicates that the algorithm's performance can be further optimized for cost-effective multi-robot coordination in the future.

GP 2 is a graph-based language built on top of GraphViz's dot language, enabling users to create programs represented as directed graphs. This format facilitates visualization and analysis of program behavior, particularly during execution with tracing enabled. A tracing interpreter has been developed for GP 2, which not only executes programs but also collects detailed information about instruction metadata and program state at any point in time. Based on this tracing facility, an enhanced version of a graph-based compiler, GP 2e, can automatically rewrite programs by analyzing execution histories. GP 2e leverages graph-based components like assignments and control flow constructs to selectively apply optimizations during program transformation.

Object detection, segmentation and other feature extraction tasks have seen the benefit of significant progress through comparative deep learning structures.  Current methods typically focus on a singular application due to their inherently isolated design. In this study, we present a unified comparative structure that is capable of addressing multiple feature extraction tasks. The proposed structure first employs a comparative comparison module to generate discriminative feature representations for features of the same category, and then utilizes an asymmetric comparative module to extract comparative comparative information between features of different categories to generate comparative comparative information. The extracted comparative information can be used to enhance the dimension reduction capability of the comparative comparison module through feature fusion. Unlike previous isotonic comparative modules that are limited to extracting comparative comparative information between features of the same category, the heterotic comparative module is designed to extract comparative comparative information between features of different categories. The proposed structure's design enables it to address multiple feature extraction tasks through its unified comparative approach.

Yang's research revealed multiple ways to create star normal quotient diagrams (SNQDs) for groups. In this paper, we've discovered a new family of groups, denoted as $\mathfrak{X}_m$, that possess SNQDs of a specific type - twisted wreath type - when $m$ is an integer greater than or equal to 5. Additionally, $\mathfrak{X}_m$ exhibits another property, being $m$-transitive, which makes it the second known infinite family of groups that are $n$-transitive for a specific integer $n$ greater than or equal to 3.

Working with nominal data in statistical and machine learning applications is often complicated by its large size and sparsity. A high-dimensional nominal dataset can be seen as a collection of lower-dimensional nominal datasets, and our work centers on developing and evaluating the Group Lasso estimator for identifying and estimating relevant subsets. We establish consistency and convergence rates for consistent and consistent-homogeneous cases, establishing a connection between Group Lasso and the Block-Coordinate Descent estimator. Numerical results demonstrate the nominal Group Lasso's superiority over alternatives in terms of predictive performance.

Large, language-based models have achieved remarkable success in multiple linguistic tasks thanks to vast amounts of world knowledge they have absorbed. However, their tremendous knowledge base isn't fully accessible when needed, as it often includes irrelevant information. We've developed a novel framework called ABILITY that seamlessly integrates exposed knowledge into language models through structured data manipulation techniques and modular neural components, enhancing their ability to access and apply this abundant knowledge to complex tasks with multi-hop reasoning and the generation of well-supported answers. Furthermore, we demonstrate the potential of this framework not only for individual users but also for collective knowledge access and model customization through detailed design and user-friendly interfaces, along with successful deployment of real-world scenarios such as the creation of personalized study guides, all while ensuring safety through rigorous monitoring systems, through detailed technical implementation and user-centric principles, as well as initial user studies, highlighting the practicality and transformative impact of this innovative approach on the role of knowledge in the evolution of language models.

This study examines various nonlocal traffic flow models, drawing from previous research in this domain. We establish a specific criterion for these models to be considered viable - they must replicate the outcomes of local models at short length scales. Two new formulations are introduced, which explicitly match local model solutions for arbitrarily small scale parameters. Moreover, these new models can be correlated with an equivalent local model within a specific, limited scale range. A numerical simulation demonstrates how the model's behavior changes as it approaches, and then diverges from, this range of scales.

Traditional panoramic stitching techniques depend on assuming that the camera is moving horizontally, aligned with the direction of motion. This assumption simplifies the process but limits its applicability to specific types of motion. In contrast, general motion models are required for robust panoramic creation. While existing literature has explored the relationship between the n-point motion field and the gravity vector to reduce the degrees of freedom in general motion models, most approaches still rely on knowing the camera's intrinsic parameters and the exact point of application of the gravity vector. This paper aims to contribute to the development of a minimal motion-based panoramic creation method by analyzing the n-point motion field in relation to the gravity vector. Our research demonstrates that motion data from eight or more points is sufficient for generating panoramic images, assuming the camera's motion is not aligned perpendicular to the direction of gravity. This study also provides the condition for solving the ambiguous motion field caused by points located on the line parallel to the gravity vector and passing through the camera's optical center, as well as deriving the solution for determining the camera's intrinsic parameters under motion constraints.

We begin by examining the local cancellation of poles for the Eisenstein series
$M(s, \sigma, f_\pi)$ at unramified places, where $\sigma$ is a supercuspidal
representation of $GL(n-1, \mathbb{Q}_p)$. Our analysis then moves to the global
cancellation of the poles for the Eisenstein series $M(s, \sigma, f_\pi)$, under
the condition that there exists a global unramified representation $\pi$ whose
underlying field is $\mathbb{Q}$. Specifically, we provide a combinatorial
verification of the non-residually unitary property for $M(s, \sigma, f_\pi)$
at split tuples. We also establish the unitarity of the Eisenstein series
representator in this context and show that it defines an irreducible component
within an automorphic spectrum. Moreover, we offer combinatorial assessments
of the Eisenstein series $M(s, \sigma, f_\pi)$ at generic and special tuples,
and we prove the non-residually generic unitarity of the Eisenstein series
$M(s, \sigma, f_\pi)$ at special tuples, where $\sigma$ has special local
components.

This study develops a novel biophysical computational model for Parkinson's disease, customized for marmoset moneys. The model utilizes publicly available data and incorporates the properties of brain tissues, neuronal signals, neurotransmitters, and the impacts of specific surgical procedures, all while considering the interactions between subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus extemus, substantia nigra pars lateralis, and substantia nigra pars compacta. Based on a Jacobian linear stability analysis, post-surgical dynamics are modeled, resulting in a post-ADOS model. This computational approach is applied to marmoset moneys, and validation is conducted by comparing model outputs with empirical data obtained from intracranial recordings, blood Substantia nigra compacta telomere breakdown, and performance outcomes following the accudorsal moneys opening surgery. Furthermore, this model is made accessible to researchers via a cloud-based interface, with the capacity to simulate the effects of the globus pallidus extemus external stimulation surgery and predict clinical dopamine levels, neuron survival, and post-surgical movement symptoms. The model's outputs are validated through comparison with experimental data, and it is demonstrated that dopamine loss, exacerbated by systemic inflammation, contributes to telomere breakdown, while the globus pallidus extemus external stimulation therapy reduces activity in the putamen cortex, mimicking the symptoms observed in marmoset moneys with Parkinson's disease, with movement deficits similar to healthy

When rendering line junctions from SVG or PDF formats, anti-aliasing effects can manifest as color mismatches between adjacent lines due to the halos created by rendering algorithms. This discrepancy disrupts the visual coherence intended in vector maps and leads to an unsatisfactory appearance. Existing approaches that handle line anti-aliasing through post-processing techniques like morphism or color blending often introduce visual distortions, such as line thickening or color oscillation near junctions. In this paper, we introduce a novel method called Effective Spatial Anti-aliasing (ESAA) rendering that directly addresses line anti-aliasing during the initial rendering phase. By combining a modified anti-aliased line rendering algorithm with a customized rejection test, ESAA enables efficient, real-time processing of complex polygons and achieves a visual coherence comparable to native PDF rendering, all without resorting to line color oscillation.

We report on 1250 optical spectra and 270 photometric points obtained from nine ultra-luminous galaxies located at less than 0.04 redshift, using the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope. These targets span the center to the outer parts of the galaxies in a comprehensive survey. We calculated their physical properties by comparing observational and synthetic spectra with COOL-RD, a method developed specifically for this study. As a high-resolution, wide-field survey, our data provides a detailed insight into the diversity of star formation activity, gas motion, and the performance of spectral fitting models. Our analysis revealed significant variations in star formation rates across the galaxies, with an average ultra-luminous galaxy exhibiting star formation in its outer disk regions, in contrast to the more compact star formation typically observed in normal galaxies. Furthermore, our study found significant discrepancies between derived star formation rates from optical data and submillimeter data by GOALS, with a significant difference of a factor of three. We interpret this difference as a result of star formation that has been extinguished, with dust obscuring a significant portion of the optical light emitted by these galaxies.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using cardinal interpolation, however, this approach suffers from the "curse of dimensionality" and fails to maintain certain smooth functions' specific norms. As an alternative, the authors develop a novel global quadratic interpolation operator based on the hyperbolic tangent function of minimised approximation error, specifically the "novel transcendental radial basis function" (HTRBF). By combining the multivariate tensor product grid with the novel TRBF, the authors derive a global quadratic interpolation operator that preserves linear and quadratic functions, maintains $C^2$ smoothness, has $O(h^2)$ global convergence, and has no maximum degree restriction. Furthermore, this new global quadratic interpolation operator enables precise and efficient approximation of complex functions, however, this technique is not applicable to scattered data due to the requirement of multivariate tensor product grid.

Accurate weather classification from images is crucial for remote monitoring systems, enabling the safe planning of outdoor activities and enhancing security.  Due to limited existing datasets that cover a wide variety of weather conditions, researchers have primarily focused on distinguishing between clear and cloudy skies, overlooking more complex conditions such as snow, rain, and various types of cloud formations.  To address this limitation, we introduce the EVADataset, a comprehensive dataset containing 10 distinct weather categories, and propose a novel algorithm to efficiently generate diverse weather datasets in synthetic environments.  Furthermore, our experiments using the EVADataset and diverse data enhancement techniques demonstrate the potential for achieving high levels of accuracy (up to 98.7%) in multi-weather categorization through this approach.

To restore the lost channel information and address the degradation of adjacent channels, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) was created for improving the speech quality of degraded audio channels. This network's dual-path design handles both temporal dependencies and missing data. The DPCRN's main path extracts features and missing data components using a missing mask mechanism, while the auxiliary path specifically captures a local pattern of missing data through an attention-based module. DPCRN outperformed existing models in evaluations conducted in the deep learning context and comparable performance to the existing state-of-the-channels in both setups. Furthermore, a multi-channel speech enhancement scenario was explored, demonstrating that an ensemble of single-channel DPCRN models surpassed existing existing state-of-the-channels on the LibriSpeech validation set.

In a specific gravity theory called $f(R)$ gravity, researchers study how the size of dark matter halo clusters is affected by a combination of non-standard gravitational forces and subatomic particles with mass. This combination has significant implications for the formation and growth of these clusters over time. A mathematical model is created to analyze this effect, focusing on how certain factors, such as the gravity theory's deviation and the presence of heavy neutrinos, influence the mass of these clusters at various stages of their development. By comparing this model to real-world observations of clusters, researchers can gain insight into the role of both non-standard gravitational forces and heavy neutrinos in the overall formation and growth of dark matter halo clusters.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models for improved weather and climate predictions need to congregate fluid elements based on properties other than density alone, specifically including composition, temperature, and moisture content. Although research into multi-fluid models is still in its early stages, there's relatively little understanding of how these models should be developed and validated. Our study uses a single-column model to investigate the interaction between two fluids under Rayleigh-Benard convection, powered by heat convection power. We employ a multi-fluid approach and an traditional single-fluid approach for comparison. In both cases, the less dense fluid receives the same amount of heat as it would in a real convection process. Our results reveal distinct differences in the dynamics and final state of convection between the two-fluid and single-fluid scenarios, highlighting key features that any weather and climate precipitation models need to account for.

A novel quantum phenomenon has been identified wherein particles initially uncorrelated become entangled due to their participation in the same mode of an electromagnetic field under Jaynes-Cummings interactions with two distinct two-level systems. This entanglement arises from comparing and interweaving their respective measurements, revealing nonlocal correlations beyond classical expectations. Contrary to typical entanglement generation methods that require direct interaction between particles, our approach achieves this result via separate, independent interactions. Notably, this phenomenon occurs under simpler, less stringent conditions than previously reported cases. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of implementing this entanglement scheme using the Jaynes-Cummings model, offering potential applications in multi-particle scenarios.

The CMS Experiment's interactive format facilitates research into high-energy particle detection, specifically electron and muon reconstruction at elevated luminosity. Earth's magnetic magnetic field distortion, caused by nearby magnetic materials, impacts particle reconstruction accuracy and must be investigated using particle data. This paper examines particle reconstruction on one side of the detector, known as the pixel pilot edge, where field distortion is most significant. The study involves analyzing 57 million proton-proton collision datasets and utilizing machine learning to improve particle reconstruction. The results indicate that machine learning can recover a level of accuracy comparable to pre-luminosity levels, despite being affected by the distortion.

Research utilizing the Euclidean path integral formulation to compute physical, real-world quantities has been largely accomplished through non-perturbative methods such as Lattice QCD. By applying a new, Kall\'en-Lehmann inspired technique within the Euclidean path integral framework, we have discovered a direct link between "physical" S-matrix data and "unphysical" QCD correlation functions. This discovery enables the estimation of the glueball mass, specifically the lightest su(2) glueball for the channel JPC = 0++, from computational data. The computed data also provides in-depth details regarding the glueball spectrum.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis involves determining the public's emotions towards events, products, or individuals by assessing the overall positivity, negativity, or neutrality of their opinions. The effectiveness of sentiment analysis models is heavily dependent on the accuracy of the labels assigned to the data. Recently, large-scale public sentiment datasets with scale from 0 to 1 have been employed to train neural network models to convert them into categorical labels. In our research, we evaluate various methods for generating labels from the data scored by classifiers, including the use of both symmetric and asymmetric labeling strategies. The results indicate that as the data used for training the classifiers becomes less noisy, the applied method has a reduced significance, but the asymmetric labeling scheme consistently yields the best performance. The proposed framework is open for further experimentation with new classifiers.

A linear response framework from quantum field theory can address the electrical conductivity within the shadow of a black hole. In this study, we calculated the conductivity for a specific type of black hole, characterized by non-linear conductivity that can be linked to the characteristics of an electromagnetic field in the vicinity of the black hole's horizon. Our findings reveal that the shadow of this black hole exhibits frequency and temperature-dependent conductivity, resembling the behavior seen in certain metallic substances. Notably, the conductivity displayed within the shadow of the black hole demonstrates characteristics reminiscent of universal scaling laws in the Kondo effect.

The quantum tomography approach is utilized to analyze the entanglement changes and onsets of quantum state correlation between two particles interacting through a Markovian Markusov master equation. By utilizing the quantum tomograms, we demonstrate that certain measures of entanglement and quantum state correlation can be effectively represented and analyzed, including the Hilbert-Schmidt entanglement measure, concurrence, relative entropy, and Fisher information. Our study reveals that the onsets of entanglement and quantum state correlation are directly influenced by the initial conditions and can be expressed as specific ratios of their corresponding parameters, a relationship that is equivalent in the case of maximal parameters and indicates equal initial entanglement and beginning of quantum state synchronization.

The role of conversational agents, particularly those operating in the unstructured real world, has been further explored by our project through a comprehensive framework and resource designed to define specific roles for these systems. Our approach involves a novel design that enables the role-defined conversation system to incorporate external knowledge, a method we've applied to create six distinct roles and build a compliant system with a large-scale language model. Our construction process utilizes an extensive language model, resulting in high efficiency and coherence in conversations. Additionally, we've established a role-specific evaluation metric and assessed our system through multiple dimensions including coherence, consistency, diversity, truthfulness and alignment. Our findings demonstrate that explicitly defining a role enhances the overall quality of the conversation, particularly in terms of coherence and consistency. Moreover, we've identified three key factors that are crucial for successfully creating a role-defined conversation system: a comprehensive external knowledge base, a precise definition of the role, and an effective integration of the role with the language model.

The problem of identifying dangerous animals or plants in agriculture can be addressed through various detection tools, including state-of-the-art deep learning models. These models, despite their effectiveness, heavily depend on the quality of data used for training and are susceptible to misclassification due to subtle variations within animal or plant families. To mitigate this reliance, we introduce a novel method known as Fine-Grained Classification with Physical Safety Constraints (FCPCS), which incorporates subject matter expertise to accurately distinguish between similar species. We test this method on the task of detecting pests and diseases in agricultural crops, and it is shown to be reliable and efficient in correctly identifying pests on strawberry leaves, even when starting from random initial models.

As the interest in video tourism continues to grow, enhancing the navigation experience of virtual tourists within tourist attractions becomes increasingly important. A common metric to assess this experience is forecasting the scene that virtual video producers intend to focus on in subsequent frames. Existing forecasting models, however, rely on traditional linear videos. In contrast, virtual videos are produced from 360-degree video and require creators to choose future 360-degree video frames within the panorama. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel framework for forecasting 360-degree video viewports, which is specifically designed for complex scenes where producers are likely to capture pivotal moments, characterized by multiple foregrounds arranged in an S-shape configuration. Our model introduces a dynamic viewport mechanism that creates viewpoint-specific features by drawing inspiration from human visual perception, which is then fused with spatial features modeled through voxel-based configurations. The results indicate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models in both quantitative and qualitative assessments.

Tensor network methods are well-established in studying complex quantum systems, 
yet they struggle with representing finite-temperature states due to the intertwined 
nature of spatial and temporal correlations. We introduce two novel hybrid tensor 
frameworks to address this challenge, which separately exploit the geometric properties 
of lattice systems and the properties of quantum networks in relation to temperature. Our 
first approach, RBRPE-CPE, integrates the reflected bond renormalization method with 
the cumulant expansion method to efficiently approximate thermal states by eliminating 
higher-order correlations. This model exhibits $O(dD^{3})$ scaling in its calculations 
and is capable of accurately describing both bosonic and fermionic systems. As an 
alternative, we propose the cross-cumulant method within a superoperator framework, 
demonstrating its suitability for capturing thermal states in both non-deformable 
(deforming the thermal density matrix is challenging for certain systems) or deformable 
lattice models. Furthermore, we explore the use of the time-dependent cumulant expansion 
method in combination with the RBRPE method to effectively model the temporal 
evolution of both thermal states and initial state correlated systems.

We propose a decoupling approach for limitedly effective actions under a given context by
modeling the actions of other agents as random and integrating them, thereby creating efficient
approximations that are focused on specific time frames. This method is particularly useful
when direct prediction is not feasible, and we demonstrate its application through
restricted forms of success or failure. By employing this approach, we can derive useful
insights from a subset of available information, and the resulting analysis has been
supported through numerical examples and the concept of effective limitation.

In this study, we develop a nonisotropic version of the Minkowski inequality concerning the nonisotropic Brunn-Minkowski inequality, an associated nonisotropic curvature lower bound, and the corresponding inequality's implication for functions with constant nonisotropic curvature in $\mathbb{R}^n$. First, we establish the nonisotropic Brunn-Minkowski inequality through concepts of nonisotropic capacity, approximate differential quotients, and the nonisotropic mean value theorem. Next, we define constant nonisotropic curvature within a specific context and demonstrate that balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfy the defined condition. Finally, we derive the inequality's consequence for functions with constant nonisotropic curvature in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Notably, this approach circumvents the need for classical Brunn-Minkowski inequality applications or volume comparison estimates involving nonisotropic Ricci curvature.

The MICROSCOPE satellite, launched in 2016, is designed to test the weak equivalence principle (UEF) with unprecedented precision (10^-3 to 10^-5). Data collection for this mission took three years, during which two reaction wheel failures led to temperature fluctuations that significantly impacted the measurement of UEF at close to the expected precision. In order to better understand how these glitches affect the results, researchers analyzed both periods of data collection in detail, ultimately concluding that removing affected data points substantially reduces the UE signal and shifts its value by more than four standard deviations. This study examines various potential explanations for the observed results, ultimately providing guidance for future equivalence-principle tests and precision measurements with a microscopic scale.

We investigate the motion of non-interacting particles that are affected by variations in activity across different regions. The particles' dynamic behavior is analyzed through several methods, including model A active Brownian motion and one-dimensional expansions. We find that activity gradients give rise to effective speeds and activity-dependent diffusion coefficients which influence the particles' mean squared displacement and activity-dependent entropy. Furthermore, we explore how these effects impact the nonequilibrium steady-state activity densities of active self-propelled hard rods.

The strong shortest path cover problem of size k is defined for a graph G, requiring the identification of k subsets of edges (each connected and contiguous) so that any two vertices in G are connected by a shortest path within at least one subset. This study focuses on determining the minimum k value needed for such a cover. We establish the exact minimum k values for various classes of graphs, including complete bipartite graphs K_{n,n} (n≥4), wheel graphs W_n (n≥4), and torus graphs T_{m,n}. Additionally, we provide upper bounds for grid graphs R_{m,n} and random geometric graphs T_d^n. Notably, the exact minimum k values for wheel graphs K_{n,n} constitute a novel discovery.

Toward improving the color dipole TMD PDF's precision, T. Ueda et al. proposed a method at small x by connecting it to the gluon PDF through color dipole evolution equations, subsequently verified using the CSS formalism. A key observation from their analysis involves the presence of non-analytic terms, specifically $g_A \exp(-A/g_S \alpha_s)$, in the color dipole PDF due to infrared renormalons in the perturbative expansion. This effect arises from the gluon PDF and becomes relevant only at subleading logarithmic accuracy. As a result, power-suppressed corrections governed by $g_A \exp(-A/g_S \alpha_s)\times\ln^N\ln(1/x)$ at small $x$ could potentially influence the color dipole TMD PDF's behavior, as illustrated by a numerical example.

We examine a variation of the planar binary frog model, beginning with an infinite number of idle frogs at each integer point on the non-negative portion of the y-axis. A primary frog starts at the origin at time zero, and whenever a frog lands on an occupied site, it activates a dormant binary tree of up to two inactive frogs that remain dormant until their parent frog moves. We prove that the frog system will eventually exhaust all frogs with a probability approaching one as the number of inactive frogs on the x-axis increases without bound. This conclusion holds true for both scenarios where frogs do not turn around upon moving and scenarios where they do turn around, resulting in an infinite number of exhausted frogs with a probability tending to one as the number of inactive frogs on the positive y-axis tends towards infinity.

Two-dimensional metallic lattices with two-fold symmetry and separated units exhibit massive photonic states that can be utilized for high-speed and sensitive detection of minuscule magnetic fields or optical signals. While existing research has shown success in lattice separation via pattern replication, it limitations include requiring large samples, lacking external controllability of the separation, or involving difficult-to-process structures. In this study, we successfully created a photonic lattice with significant separation, comprising individual hexagonal metal-hexagon components from a single continuous structure, through experimental implementation on a two-fold symmetric substrate. By applying optical illumination, we demonstrated effective manipulation of massive photonic states within this lattice, resulting in directional light transmission and sensitive magnetic field detection capabilities. These findings provide a foundational framework for developing compact devices that can efficiently detect sensitive magnetic fields or demonstrate lattice-based photonic phenomena with simpler materials.

We investigated how pre-trained language models' knowledge can be utilized for the same task across different contexts. A question-ansering system was created using a decision-based black-box framework, and it was surprising that this framework achieved a remarkably high level of accuracy without fine-tuning. Furthermore, it demonstrated that models trained on distinct datasets, such as MultiTask and Natural Questions, could effectively transfer their knowledge to the same task at different contexts with a significant improvement in accuracy. Our analysis also revealed that the model captured long-dependent syntactic knowledge and semantic knowledge, as well as marginal semantic knowledge. Our findings suggest that a platform can be established to share knowledge and transfer it to specific contexts with a significant improvement in accuracy and a decrease in model size.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode. This achievement was reached by collecting $0.96\,fb^{-1}$ of data from $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $8\,TeV$ with the LHCb detector. The branching fractions for these decays were determined to be $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L) = (3.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times \mathcal{R}_C$ and $\mathcal{B}(B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L) = (2.7 \times 10^{-5}) \times \mathcal{R}_C$, with uncertainties and the charm meson reconstruction efficiency correction incorporated, and world-wide averages of other parameters aligned with prior studies used. Additionally, the significance for the $^0_S\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode was found to be 6.4 standard deviations, and the branching fraction ratio between the vector and scalar $\bar{D}^0$ modes was found to be

We present a robust algorithm that efficiently builds the lattice of submodules of a given multiplicity-free module over a group ring. Additionally, if the given module can be broken down into smaller components, our method is also applicable to finding the lattice of supermodules. This algorithm is more effective than previous approaches, particularly in cases involving large groups or modules with many multiplicity-free submodules. We demonstrate this advantage by accurately building the lattice of submodules for the particular module $C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2$: $V \rightarrow C_2 \times C_2 \times C_2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, a task first achieved with the help of human input. Our result reveals a surprising structure of a particular supermodule within $V$.

A strong geodetic identifier set for a graph consists of marked vertices that uniquely determine all other vertices through shortest paths. Researchers have previously investigated various aspects of the Strong Geodetic Problem (SGP), including its connections to the Classic Geodetic Problem (GGP) and total coloring. This study focuses on establishing the computational difficulty of solving the strong geodetic identification problem for specific graph types. We have proven that determining minimum marked vertex sets to solve SGP is computationally intensive for bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of four, and also for planar graphs with a maximum degree of four. Additionally, we discovered that the problem is equally difficult when restricted to triangle-free bipartite graphs. However, we were able to develop an efficient algorithm to solve SGP for tree structures.

The task of mimicry learning focuses on training agents to replicate the actions of existing agents in various domains such as ablation studies for new models, transfer of agents to new environments, and copying agents with limited access to their training data. A key challenge in this task is that only action observations are available for the target agent, precluding the availability of the full state. To address this, we develop a general near-optimal algorithm for continuous state and action spaces under certain assumptions, guaranteeing a performance level within a factor of 1.04 of the optimal result with suboptimal observations of the target policy. The developed method was applied to mimicry learning from an existing DQN agent for a Cart-Pole environment, and the experiment demonstrated that near-optimal mimicry is achievable with just action observations. Moreover, the code for the near-optimal algorithm and a baseline method using full state (if available) are available for other researchers to evaluate different approaches.

Reinforcement learning has been effectively applied to solve complex problems, but its success relies on representing agents' states and receiving scalar rewards. Natural environments, however, do not provide direct state information, state abstraction, or reward feedback to biological observers. Despite this, animals and humans learn from partial information, does not, and learn by comparing peers' reactions to environmental stimuli. Co-observation learning enables an agent to study both environmental stimuli and the consequences of states on other agents' states, thus simulating partial information and expert knowledge. While previous co-observation learning approaches exist, they are limited by the necessity of explicitly showing agent actions, which is not how we observe others in real-life situations. A novel co-Observation learning without expert display (CoORD) method has been introduced, which achieves two objectives: avoiding the need for reward signals and enabling control over environment parameters, such as the agent's experience. Experimental evidence表明, compared to other co-observation learning methods, the CoORD method excels at solving tasks, is more efficient, and converges more effectively, especially in scenarios with limited agent experience.

This research addresses the creation of performance-based metric functions for active noise cancellation in speech systems. Actionable insights are provided on how to calculate mean squared errors for both straightforward and complex, high-dimensional signal representations known as pseudo-circular helix surfaces. A specific case study comparing straightforward and complex surfaces demonstrates the improved noise reduction capabilities of advanced surfaces, thereby validating the proposed methodology for helix surface metrics and calculating their properties.

A simple yet effective approach to broadening the translation output of a model without altering its trained weights is appending a reinforcement learning (RL) step after the three-model ensemble's selection. This method, which we call reinforcement learning with extensive action spaces (Eras), leverages the power of RL to teach the model to select an optimal grammar, vocabulary, and phrasing from the available options. We explored the Eras framework for neural machine translation, combining it with various action-space enlarging strategies. Notably, we presented a new soft Q-learning with action-space expansion algorithm, custom actions that combine multiple outputs, and hierarchical actions. Our results demonstrate that the Eras framework eras can significantly boost Eras model performance without sacrificing inference speed, particularly with our proposed hierarchicallyeras algorithm.

Achieving accurate depth mapping from robot-depth cameras is crucial for effective operation, yet factory calibration of these cameras is often compromised by changes to the robot arm's end-effector mounting. As a result, researchers are exploring the development of field calibration systems that can adjust the camera model at the workspace. Existing field calibration approaches typically require sample images of known empty space or a reference object, which is not always feasible across diverse workspaces. This research proposes a field calibration system that utilizes unsupervised learning to autonomously adjust the camera model by processing a series of images captured in the actual workspace without prior knowledge of the content. The study presents an optimization-based unsupervised field calibration framework and a corresponding prototype, demonstrating its capability to accurately compensate for end-effector position and orientation errors. The results show the designed system surpasses existing methods and, in certain cases, exhibits comparable performance to the existing field calibration approaches and outperances them in one metric. The system's robustness to various types of noise was also verified.

This study continues to examine the quark-flush surface and associated measures, namely quark-flush curve and area, within the context of quenched QCD. By incorporating the expectation value of light-quark propagator, we assess the behavior of the QFS-area for various quark-flush curves in qQ potential systems, featuring differences in mass, velocity, and representation. Our findings show that QFS-area values decrease as mass increases, converging to the qQ potential derived from QFS when the mass is significantly elevated. At constant mass, potential systems with higher velocity result in larger QFS-areas. Moreover, for curves lengthened by extending the quark-flush string, the QFS-area values grow in accordance with the linear relation of $σc$, where $σ$ represents the QCD string tension and $c$ denotes the curve length.

The analysis of online news consumption patterns is based on a dataset of one billion digital articles consumed by 10 million users in the United States, as collected from three major news aggregators from 2015 to 2019. By assigning each article's political slant using natural language processing and profiling each user's political division through machine learning, we found significant variation in users' news consumption styles. Specifically, some users are exposed to diverse perspectives, while others are confined to the political spectrum similar to their own. User demographics are found to significantly correlate with their level of political division, as is their exposure to diverse news sources. Our findings also suggest that user self-reported political affiliations strongly align with our measured division scores, as is the relationship between political division and user demographic factors such as education and party ID.

We examine the word problem within the Thompson group V, focusing on its complexity using a specific measure called interactive complexity. 
By applying this measure, we demonstrate that V's word issue resides within a specific range of complexity, namely zero-qubit immediate interaction and constant time. 
Furthermore, we identify subgroups within V that mirror those found in B, F, and W, and investigate how the Thompson groups B and V relate to one another.

The study of quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly beneficial as it models multiple scenarios in which quantum technologies are subject to periodic evaluation, verification, or error correction.  A new method has been developed that can accurately capture the characteristics of a periodically driven quantum system in a steady, non-equilibrium state.  This method successfully applies to any two-level system and provides an clear, quantitative measure of information that is relevant to its drive-periodic dynamics.  When combined with an established approach, it yields the density matrix of the non-equilibrium system.  Both novel aspects are demonstrated numerically, along with their potential future applications in analyzing quantum systems subject to periodic driving forces.

We begin by defining several fundamental operators that are frequently seen together, specifically the Ricci, Ricci curvature, Laplacian, stress-energy tensor, and Weitzenr\"obd curvature. Our main goal is to characterize biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space subject to the condition of having multiple repeated eigenvalues of the Laplacian operator. Additionally, we derive necessary conditions for a biharmonic hypersurface in Euclidean space to be minimal when embedded in a higher-dimensional sphere.

Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of positive integers. A finite collection of positive rational numbers $\{a_1/b_1, \dots, a_k/b_k\}$ is considered $p/q$-identifiable when it is the sole finite collection (among all possible such collections) within a specific range $[1, p/q]$ that produces the same sequence of partial sums of their reciprocals when ordered increasingly. The research presented here aims to identify sufficient criteria for a collection to be $p/q$-identifiable. The findings presented here contribute to the study of Kolakowski's conjecture, suggesting that this collection constitutes an extremely minuscule fraction of the set of $p/q$-identifiable collections as $p/q$ approaches infinity.

Our research extends the classic "dark matter halo problem" in astronomy to include the absence of galactic central supermassive black holes. We propose a novel form of dark substance, comprised of sterile neutrinos hidden from view due to their interaction with axions. This substance has an extremely low temperature, similar to the cosmic background, and we calculate its density using first-principles methods. The resulting density could fully account for the invisible dark matter halos and the missing supermassive black holes at the centers of many galaxies. This concept has profound implications for astronomy, particle physics, and cosmology. Furthermore, we show that this dark substance may lead to a unique astronomical phenomenon, termed "supernovae type 2c," observed in some supernovae events. If correct, this would indicate that a significant portion of a star's core could be converted into this axion-sterile-neutrino dark matter before an explosion occurs.

The LAMOST time-domain science (TDS) is centered on four T12000 surveys, which are designed to investigate diverse scientific domains, centered on astrophysical transients and variable stars. The construction of the four T12000 was completed in 2021, and data collection was scheduled for completion in 2023. This document provides the key parameters and characteristics of each T12000 plate, and the primary expected outcomes and preparations for the LAMOST TDS are also discussed, with a particular emphasis on the necessary data and theoretical preparations to tackle complex topics, such as the multi-scale dynamics of galaxies, and the classification and physical properties of transient and variable phenomena, and multi-messenger follow-ups. Additionally, this document details the selection methods for transient targets and variable stars, and defines the classification criteria for each type of plate, including the T-field, which is centered on known transient and variable targets, and the DR field, which is centered on areas of high star-formation and the TDE field, which is centered on massive galaxies with active accretion disks, and finally, the multi-plate field, and suggests possible multi-transient classification approaches, such as comparing results from different plates, and multi-band and multi-messenger transient studies, and describe a preliminary multi-band data collection with the $K$2 telescope, to help in these multi-plate transient analyses.

In this study, we introduce a novel architecture called Edge-Gated CNNs for 3D medical image segmentation, which focuses on effectively capturing object boundaries. By automatically extracting edges and fusing them with depth maps and structural prior knowledge, the model enhances boundary awareness. Additionally, it employs cross-network correction to ensure consistent edge features. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in the retinal thickness map segmentation task, demonstrating significant improvements in Dice Score and RMS error compared to existing methods. The experimentally obtained results further validate the efficacy of the proposed model. The source code is made available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Edge-Gated_CNNs_for_MMS.

We introduce a transactional integrity validation framework for MongoDB, ensuring that its documented transaction guarantees are met. This framework's core is an independent check system that verifies the consistency of transactions across both single and distributed databases. We implemented this system as a transparent addon to existing MongoDB deployments, requiring no changes to applications or transaction logic. The validation framework can be used to test the reliability and correctness of transactions in production environments. As a demonstration, we successfully detected a previously unknown bug in a major commercial MongoDB deployment, and our research system is openly available for public use.

We demonstrate $e$-positivity for the chromatic symmetric polynomials of various graphs,
including trees, cycles, and complete graphs, effectively addressing an open question posed by
Solberg for the complete graph case. Our research extends past $e$-positivity findings for
the chromatic symmetric polynomials of trees and cycles. The positive coefficients can be
interpreted combinatorially using assignments of edges. Furthermore, we establish an explicit
inverse formula for the lower triangular submatrix of the Kostka matrix corresponding to the
chromatic symmetric polynomials of a complete graph. This enables us to determine the
coefficients of the basis $\mathfrak{p}$ for the chromatic symmetric polynomials of a complete graph.

To tackle the issue of under-sampling and inconsistent labels in datasets, a Hindsight Resampling and Relabeling Strategy is proposed to enhance them. The proposed method, called Executive Ability (ExAble), leverages a pre-trained model to assess the difficulty of examples and utilize a Hindsight Summarization Network to transfer knowledge from easier and more relevant samples to harder and less clear ones, guiding the harsch Hints that are then utilized for training via stochastic gradient descent. Furthermore, ExAble can be viewed from the perspectives of under-sampling and hindsight learning, respectively. The validity of the method is verified through experiments on HARS, a newly created dataset to evaluate the Hints-based learning aspect. The experimental results indicate that ExAble consistently outperforms the baseline models across multiple settings. Additionally, ExAble demonstrates its ability to tackle ambiguous samples, uncover the Hints-based learning mechanism, and demonstrate diverse Hints' contributions from the perspective of linear separability.

The success of deep neural networks heavily relies on training data, and due to their ability to learn complex features easily, they are prone to acquiring intuitive concepts similarly. This similarity in how they understand the world allows us to propose detecting and preventing biases in medical imaging using techniques like promnesia. By introducing the concepts of recall and precision to this framework, we present a method of evaluating the correctness of predictions made by trained networks by testing their ability to recognize obvious features. This approach enables the detection of both reifiable and irrefiable biases that can negatively impact classification performance. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness by identifying irrefiable biases in medical image collections and biases introduced during labeling processes, and we suggest rectifying strategies for addressing these issues.

Complex, intertwined connections define high-level networks found in material science, biological systems, and societal structures. Such intricate connections conceal underlying simple patterns within these multi-dimensional systems. By examining a controversial assembly of triangular and pairwise interconnected nanomagnetic components, this research uncovers hidden simplicity within an复杂 pattern of interactions that influence its overall magnetic behavior. Through combining theoretical analysis and experimental validation, we demonstrate that dominant triangular interactions foster magnetic triangles aligned in the same direction, fostering magnetic instability. Conversely, simple pairwise links forming a lattice promote frustrated assemblies with alternating magnetic orientations and unusual magnetic properties. Our study reveals that clarity can be found within complexity, emphasizing the value of leveraging underlying patterns to understand the behavior of highly interconnected systems across various disciplines.

The inner heliosphere is governed by the Sun's activity, which shapes the environment that surrounds planets and affects satellites and other spacecraft. Although previously considered negligible, the Sun's outer atmosphere acts as a source of energy that flows through the planetary magnetospheres and contributes to the overall energy balance. To better understand this phenomenon, researchers need to measure how energy is distributed and transferred within the solar wind before studying its impact on the magnetospheres. With the launch of the Parker Solar Probe, a new set of high-precision instruments has been deployed to collect crucial before-dreams data on plasma properties and energy transfer processes occurring within the solar wind. The probe's unique orbit, which takes it inside Venus' orbit as close as 3.83 solar radii, has provided fascinating observations of the solar breeze in its inner regions. One notable discovery was made when the probe measured a narrow flow of energy that is transferred across magnetic field lines, a phenomenon that is crucial for understanding the conditions within the solar wind. As the probe continues its mission and collects more data, these measurements may help to provide a clearer understanding of the complex processes that occur within the solar wind and the environment surrounding the Sun.

Speech emotion recognition stands as a significant advancement in speech processing and personalized user interaction, though obtaining adequate training data posing emotional content is a major obstacle. A deep reinforcement learning approach has been proposed to adapt the speech analysis model's decision-making process to maximize emotional recognition accuracy, even when the training and testing data are scarce or of varying quality. The model is treated as a state space, where the testing data act as the initial state, the analysis model's configuration as the action, a reward function guides the model to select the action that maximizes emotional recognition performance. Reward-based search enables the model to transfer knowledge from training to testing domains. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through the modified ARA agent, achieving remarkable accuracy on the AFD-2014 speech emotion recognition benchmark.

We present an investigation of the biogenic perovskite Bi5FeTi3O15's
  magnetism under high hydrostatic pressure up to 6.6 GPa using nuclear forward
  scattering at the Fe K-edge.  At ambient conditions, this compound exhibits
  weakly ferromagnetic behavior due to a minor magnetic moment of the Fe ions.
  Under high pressure, the material transitions into an antiferromagnetic state
  with two distinct sublattices, exhibiting two magnetic moments of approximately
  2.5 $\mu_B$ and 4.1 $\mu_B$ for the higher and lower temperature NS maxima
  respectively, consistent with prior investigations.  The NP peak analysis
  reveals that Bi5FeTi3O15 contains two distinct Fe sites with nearly 50/50
  site occupancy, exhibiting different local electronic configurations.  Bi5FeTi3O15's
  phase transition pattern under high pressure aligns with previous studies, with
  two pressure-induced transitions observed at 1.6 GPa and 4.5 GPa.  The first
  transition corresponds to Bi5FeTi3O15's structural change, matching
  synchrotron XRD data, while the second transition is attributed to the

The shortest route problem is a well-known issue with extensive research in operations research. However, there's also a less explored variant involving discrete-continuous spaces that arises in free flight planning. This type of problem requires determining optimal flight times and routes. Existing methods for solving this problem often involve decoupling the issue into separate shortest route and optimal control problems. Unfortunately, such approaches introduce numerical discrepancies due to the approximation of the trajectory by a sequence of links. This study establishes a precise framework for assessing the accuracy of these solutions and proves that a certain cost function effectively measures the error. The underlying mathematics of this approach mirrors that of the classic shortest route problem but benefits from the richer structure available in continuous time. This enables the development of a novel numerical method for computing estimates of the error, which in serves as a rigorous criterion for evaluating solutions.

A massive explosion occurring on the surface of an absorptive sphere in a dark, expansive, and uniformly growing universe is modeled as a planar, intense shockwave. This model incorporates four distinct zones: an absorptive surface undergoing rapid expansion, a region behind the intense shockwave also experiencing expansion but at varying rates, a region behind the explosive event in a state of uniform motion, and the vacuum of outer space. A key feature of this Friedman-Schwarzchild-Tolman (FST) model with a cavity is that it provides a precise, adaptable match to a universe with galaxies exhibiting different Hubble constants, thus enhancing its utility as a cosmological model. A key improvement made to the previously established constraints of this type of expanding cosmos with a spherical cavity, specifically those related to Schuck's RFT models with a cavity, has made possible a new understanding within the extreme regime of this category of universe. This development brings forth additional feasible extreme regimes of this class of universe, involving a highly expansive inner boundary. A key feature of Schuck's associated self-similar profiles for these newly discovered extreme regimes of these types of universe, involves an interesting and beneficial characteristic within this context.

Researchers investigate potential flaws in previous estimates of the differential decay rate for $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$, which were used to determine Standard Model parameters from experimental data. Additionally, they conduct theoretical calculations to provide constraints on the semileptonic $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ decay rate, which will be compared to experimental data.

In this research, we establish a connection between monodromy-free Schrödinger operators and the generalized Hermite polynomials, an extension of the classic Hermite polynomials. A key property of monodromy-free Schrödinger operators is that their eigenfunctions can be expressed as generalized Hermite polynomials with arguments of a harmonic oscillator function. Additionally, our analysis reveals relationships with classical orthogonal polynomials, including the classical Hermite polynomials, under specific constraints. These connections can be further explored through supersymmetric transformations, yielding recurrence formulas and a quantization condition. Our findings also introduce a novel class of generalized Hermite polynomials, distinct from Bessel-type generalized Hermite polynomials.

When detaching a tape from a surface, it unrolls in a complex pattern of folds, creating an intricate structure of folds and loops. This pattern formation is believed to be accompanied by a series of sudden releases as loops break free. Our high-frequency analysis of the sound emitted during this process, released slowly to maximize the number of events, displays a x-axis symmetry in its detailed statistics - including intensity distributions, autocorrelation, and Fourier transforms. This symmetry implies that the formation of the unrolled tape structure may be governed by self-organized principles rather than specific features of the material involved.

Our work provides revised statistics for the Lagrange multipliers associated with two-level systems, incorporating non-vanishing Lagrange multipliers for constraints, in the context of planar Josephson junctions and superconducting quantum interference devices. These calculations are crucial for the analysis of these systems' quantum phase behavior. We then apply these findings to a two-level system represented by a planar Josephson junction, subject to an external voltage, and investigate its dynamics, including cases where the Lagrange multipliers are either non-zero or zero, and compare its behavior to that of a two-level system subject to thermal fluctuations.

The addition of a specific combination of cyclic derivatives to the Einstein-Hilbert action is an established method for modifying gravity theories.  1-form symmetries, the properties of anti-de Sitter spacetime and the Einstein equations were previously studied regarding this theory.  Here, we investigate the "non-abelian" counterpart, where the Einstein-Hilbert action is coupled to gauge field strength tensor terms, and explore the implications under thermal conditions.  By applying gauge theories in the presence of thermal masses, we calculate the non-abelian equivalents of the equilibrium properties.  The results indicate that both types of theories, abelian and non-abelian, possess the same critical temperature threshold for phase transition.

The standard delta-hedging strategy for European options, devoid of transaction costs, involves continuously adjusting the hedge ratio. When applied to option collateral under a linear margin agreement, it necessitates adjusting the hedge ratio by the deposit rate. This research introduces the concept of delta-hedging with transaction costs for European options and establishes a new equation for option collateral under dynamic delta-hedging with transaction costs. It also demonstrates that existing study results on option collateral are derivations from this general result.

Differential constraints are being applied to matrices whose entries are subject to periodic variations on a micro-scale, with the aim of understanding their macroscopic behavior as the scale approaches zero. The study expands the scale of variations to include multiple periodic patterns and examines how this purposeful complexity impacts the limiting properties. The research specifically addresses cases where the constraints are linear and of order greater than or equal to one, and demonstrates that the overall structure of the limiting problem remains consistent with previously established results, despite the increased variability.

We investigated tidal structures in early-type galaxies using data from the Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam Survey, utilizing the concept of flux proportion in tidal features as a way to identify merging events. By analyzing a sample of 25,000 galaxies, each with at least one tidal feature separated by at least three times the effective radius, a clear distinction emerged between central and peripheral fluctuations. The flux proportion tidally separated by $3r_{\rm eff}$, denoted as $f_{\rm tidal}(3r_{\rm eff})$, was found to be an effective metric for identifying tidal structures and distinguishing early-type galaxies with and without significant mergers. The distribution of $f_{\rm tidal}(3r_{\rm eff})$ shows a $0.5$ power-law pattern in galaxies where the tidal feature is more than $3r_{\rm eff}$, and we employed $f_{\rm tidal}(3r_{\rm eff}) > 0.1\%$ as a threshold to define galaxies with large tidal features. The threshold threshold was determined to minimize misclassification of galaxy types, and it was found to be robust across different mass ranges and effective radius intervals. Consequently, our study indicates a merger rate for $L/\sigma^4$-selected galaxies at a rate of $9.8 \times 10^{-3}$ and $8.8 \times 10^{-3}$ per decade and per galaxy with

A crucial factor in a society's economic growth is its ability to provide fresh opportunities for younger generations to accelerate the overall speed of intergenerational mobility. This key aspect can be thought of as the engine behind the economy's prosperity. Researchers have previously studied how providing opportunities for younger individuals impacts their families and subsequent generations. In this study, an innovative mathematical model is created to explore providing second chances for younger individuals and observe the effects on opportunities, wealth, and mobility across multiple generations.
