This study introduces a novel mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow through a fractured porous medium, where the rock's permeability changes significantly across fracture surfaces. By applying a specific numerical quadrature rule to the fracture transport equations, we develop a precise approximation of the fracture pressure, which is continuous within each individual segment. Our approach effectively handles situations involving an arbitrary number of fractures in three-dimensional space, extending existing theoretical limits to include very high viscosity fluids, such as those found in oil recovery processes. Numerical experiments are provided to validate our method and illustrate its practical applications in formulating discrete pressure fields for complex flow scenarios.

To develop high-performance spintronics devices, obtaining magnetic layers with both large spin polarization and uncompensated magnetization is crucial. In this study, we examine a configuration consisting of two magnetic layers with opposite magnetizations and distinct spiral structures, situated between normal metal contacts that possess spiral magnetic order. When the spiral structures in the magnetic layers are reversed, a significant difference in resistance is observed, amounting to hundreds of percent difference, due to the creation of a unique spin accumulation pattern at the interface with spiral magnetic order that possesses extremely high polarization. This phenomenon gives rise to a highly sensitive spin-valve effect, resulting in opposite resistance variations as a function of the spiral structure in one magnetic layer. Moreover, this effect persists across different spiral structure transition points in the partially transparent spin-orbit coupled layer, leading to potential applications in spin-valve diodes. Notably, this effect is produced using only a single type of helical magnetic layer.

New statistical concepts for overcoming the limitations of Bayes Factors in
large-scale simulations and real-world data have been recently proposed. To
fully utilize these innovations, the development of appropriate computational
workflows is a crucial next step. In this study, we explore various approaches
to defining these workflows through an examination of Bayes Factors' potential
applications and limitations. Considering factors such as the source of data,
statistical modeling, theoretical basis, and evolving best practices, we outline
several strategies for updating Bayes Factors in data sets of all sizes. Among
these strategies are isolated, interlinked, and hybrid approaches that reflect
different levels of cooperation within the statistical community. To address the
challenge of open-source software integration, we introduce a customizable
Bayes Factor workflow using Reusable Statistical Workflows (RSW) and provide a
practical example using the classic Monkey See, Monkey Do simulation. Ultimately,
to fully utilize these innovative statistical concepts, the development of
community-driven best practices for the sharing and transparency of computational
workflows is crucial.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "hence" are frequently
employed in written texts to signify connections between sentences, yet their
actual utility in facilitating comprehension has been inconsistently supported
by various studies.  This research seeks to examine the diverse nature of
discourse indicators across numerous genres through a comprehensive analysis
based on large-scale semantic representations created by BERT.  Our findings
reveal that the way discourse indicators function varies significantly
depending on context and genre, and they often operate by connecting both
preceding and following text, as well as combining multiple elements.  To
discourse indicators' complex and interconnected nature, we propose a novel
approach known as Discourse Sense Evaluation (DiscSense), and we provide a
substantial dataset comprising over one million instances of discourse sense
classifications.  Our study demonstrates that the latent semantic structures
of discourses vary significantly, and basic machine learning techniques can
effectively capture this variability.  Visualizations and detailed statistical
findings are made available to facilitate future investigations into the
hidden meanings of discourse indicators.

We have conducted elevated temperature spectroscopy of the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond from K to over 300C.  By measuring the zero-phonon line shift and excited state lifetime as temperature changes, our results indicate a substantial decrease in the excited state lifetime at higher temperatures with a fitted activation energy in the 1.1eV - 1.5eV range, which is consistent with an electron-phonon interaction.  An analysis based on an tilde-S state model shows that the anisotropic part of the electron-phonon interaction may cause a significant shift in the fluorescence peak in certain directional configurations, which could be utilized to measure temperature with greater accuracy.  Furthermore, our findings in the 100C - 300C range with an adjusted electron-phonon interaction model are highly relevant for understanding and optimizing the performance of optical temperature sensors based on the NV center.

The brains of animals and humans process information through complex networks of neural connections that vary across different areas and individuals. Lower-level neural circuits, like cortical microcircuits, perform fundamental processing tasks and regulate higher-level functions. Despite over a century of study, the ways in which these circuits regulate and process information remain largely unknown. Recent advancements in mapping technical techniques have significantly improved our understanding of how individual cortical neurons and their connections function, setting the stage for a more in-depth exploration of neural circuitry. In this study, we utilized these technological breakthroughs in combination with sophisticated analytical methods to investigate how a small group of neurons, known as intralaminar thalamus (ILT), modulates activity in a section of the visual cortex called V1. We specifically focused on an area in V1 that processes motion, known as the direction-selective circuit (DSC). Our experiments revealed that when neurons in V1 were stimulated with moving patterns, they responded by activating or inhibiting their neighboring neurons, depending on the pattern of motion. We discovered that the ILT neurons played a crucial role in suppressing excessive activity in the DSC, allowing it to remain within a balanced state. When we removed this regulatory function of the ILT, we observed uncontrolled excitatory activity emerging in certain parts of the circuit. Our simulations showed that a mathematical model of an area of motion called the middle supralaminar thalamus could effectively suppress excessive activity in the DSC and restore the stability of the

Investigating the SU(3) spin system on a triangular lattice, we employ the exact su(3) symmetry within a sigma-model approach to assess the long-range magnetic interactions, or moments, of the spin types using the numerical path integral technique. Our method involves the stochastic estimation of SU(3) group elements at the lattice bonds within an auxiliary field formulation, circumventing the phase-winding problems associated with the conventional projection of spin states. This technique yields exceptionally precise valence bond degeneracy measurements for spin states up to the SU(infinity) level at zero flux on a 12x12x12 lattice. Notably, our results reveal that two-moment correlations oscillate with varying SU(n) symmetry, exhibiting no clear average pattern. As a result, the magnetic field arrangement that maximizes stability in its minimum energy state remains unclear even within reasonable SU(3) symmetry.

A new version of the HF-Spline technique has been developed to efficiently solve the Hartree-Fock equations for systems with central, spherically symmetric potentials. By separating the Hamiltonian into universal central and system-specific external parts, variations in external potential do not necessitate recalculating the HF-Spline foundations. This technique was applied to solve the HF equations for various systems, including atoms (He, Li+, Be2+, B3+, C4+, C5+, O6+, O7+, Ar16+), clusters (He2+...Ar183+), and electron gas, by comparing total energies and orbital occupancies to existing literature results. Results show our method yields more accurate results than previous HF-Spline approaches, with substantial improvements (up to 3 orders of magnitude) in accuracy for atoms and clusters, and 2 orders of magnitude for electron gas. These results demonstrate the robustness of the HF-Spline technique for solving the HF equations with central, spherically symmetric potentials.

The timing of events in highly interconnected systems of oscillators that release energy is standard in many nature phenomena. We propose a novel universality framework for predicting when events occur in these interconnected systems of oscillators, regardless of the underlying network structure, interactions, or types of oscillators. This framework consists of a set of critical parameters, and we demonstrate its broad applicability by examining situations involving fireflies, librining lasers, and cardiac cells. A specific parameter space is defined for each situation, and we provide the boundaries of this space through analytical, numerical, and experimental approaches. Our findings expand on previous research by providing the first experimental validation of this explosive synchronization phenomenon in cardiac cells, as well as a comprehensive theoretical model for the release-inhibited oscillators. The established standards for event releases can facilitate the design of safe and efficient synchronized systems of oscillators, benefiting applications in cardiac pacing and fireworks displays.

Low-rank matrix optimization applications often employ decomposition methods to reduce their complexity.
Although these methods are commonly used, their lack of convexity hinders the development of reliable and efficient optimization algorithms.
By integrating a geodesic metric from Riemannian geometry, we reexamine low-rank matrix decomposition and discover that it defines a convex structure.
Specifically, we show that any local minimum of a general nonconvex function isachieved at an extreme point of a geodesically convex landscape and prove sufficient conditions for unconstrained optimization problems.
Our theoretical findings reveal that sufficient conditions for fixed-point convergence can be satisfied even when a function has only cubic smoothness and constraints, which are more relaxed than previously known conditions that assume functions are smooth and unconstrained.
Numerical experiments on image completion and matrix factorization for recommendation systems demonstrate the validity of our sufficient conditions and provide a practical guide for selecting initialization parameters in optimization algorithms.

In a recent study by Kostochka, Yilma, and Zhu, it was proven that many bipartite cubic graphs have a notable property, but the proof excluded bipartite graphs. In this research, we establish that almost all cubic graphs, regardless of bipartiteness, share this characteristic, yet the robustness of the claim requires more evidence for bipartite graphs. We provide the first extensive set of counterexamples to the original argument, focusing particularly on bipartite graphs, and present methods to generate infinitely many such counterexamples while preserving specific subgraph structures. Additionally, we introduce algorithmic procedures for producing these counterexamples and the largest known example to date, surpassing 2 billion edges.

Identities of the Dirichlet L-functions have significant implications in number theory.
Orthogonal bases within the space of Dirichlet characters are instrumental in defining these identities.
Initially formulated by P. L. Chebyshev and subsequent researchers, the definition employed classical multiplicative characters.
We establish several new identities by utilizing the more comprehensive set of Dirichlet characters that are orthogonal over the group of Dirichlet characters.
The new identities, derived from the completeness relation and character sum properties, include expressions for the zeta function and Dirichlet L-functions with applications in prime number theory.
Specifically, they enable a novel derivation of the PNT, the PAC, the MTT, and the Dirichlet's Nonprincipal Theorem about primes in arithmetic progressions, along with a mean value theorem for the Dirichlet's prime oscillating function.
This method yields a more concise proof than the existing ones, and we demonstrate that all complex rho zeros from the set $\frac{k}{q-1}+i\frac{a}{q}$, where $\gcd(k,a,q)=1$ and $|a|<\frac{q-1}{2}$, cause the right-hand sides of our identities to vanish, thereby influencing the prime distribution in arithmetic progressions.

We explore a new beyond Standard Model (BSM) particle physics sector that interacts minimally with the Standard Model, potentially accessible in future neutrino observatories like CTAE and CTAN. This new sector, consisting of several types of particles, is mass-dependent and could be discovered through the analysis of neutrino and air shower data. Specifically, we focus on very heavy BSM particles with masses dependent on up to 10^6 GeV. Despite their high mass, these particles are unstable and would result in decays that produce high-energy neutrinos. The distance these particles travel before decaying is dependent on their lifetime and would depend on as much as 10^6 times their inverse mass squared. The analysis of air showers and neutrinos may provide evidence for these particles based on specific characteristics such as energy distributions, ratios of charged currents to extensive air showers, and excesses of neutrinos that match certain directional and energy criteria.

The viscoelastic properties of a fluid significantly influence the movement of spherical organisms that swim using viscoelastic materials.  A previously developed model with viscoelastic properties was modified by adding a second differential equation describing the materials properties.  However, the viscoelastic model required simplifying assumptions that limited its accuracy.  In this study, we explored how swimming patterns, especially in terms of speed and direction changes, affected trilinear swimmers using both elastic and viscoelastic materials.  Our results revealed that viscoelastic properties caused asymmetry in swimming forward and backward, with a larger impact on swimming backward.  By analyzing torque, we found that viscoelastic forces acted differently on the front and rear sections of the swimmer, contributing to the observed asymmetry.  In contrast, elastic forces provided a balanced impact.  Interestingly, we discovered that swimming backward was faster than in the corresponding elastic case, while the viscoelastic properties slowed the forward swim.  Furthermore, restoring the viscoelastic forces to their elastic counterparts was possible by adjusting the asymmetry in viscoelastic resistance.  Our findings provide valuable insights into how viscoelastic properties impact swimming movement and can be applied to understand biological movement in various environments.

We investigated how symmetric Cournot game-evolving genetic algorithms with varying configurations compare to a specific state in a single, asymmetric Cournot game. Specifically, we analyzed whether they exhibit similar performance around a given Nash equilibrium. We found that certain genetic algorithm settings produce similar results to those in the single, asymmetric game, and these successful configurations always result in populations displaying similar mean and variance outcomes to an equally informed market. Furthermore, we observed that successful configurations are robust to minor perturbations when applied to the single, asymmetric game, and they yield similar high-quality solutions to a Cournot game with participants having varying levels of market information.

Despite being utils for knowledge extraction from natural language processing,
existing studies lack consideration of ontology enrichment from processed text.
To bring about new value from structurally undefined data sources, this paper
investigates the utilization of neural network-based methods to discover novel
connections within OWA, thereby augmenting existing knowledge ontologies.
To demonstrate this, we utilized OWA31 as a case study, employing a neural
network method to identify implicit relations in natural language annotations,
which led to an increase in OWA31's relations by 14.5% at minimal additional
cost to system developers. This approach can be utilized to enrich existing
ontologies, which in turn can provide significant benefits to downstream tasks
in the field of NLP.

A novel mechanism has been proposed to combine Ising and voter models, potentially representing a fundamental building block for nonequilibrium systems that exhibit both competition and cooperation, with interesting properties related to critical phenomena. This mechanism is an Ising-quenched voter model, with different types of Heisenberg interactions varying from competition to cooperation, and a common external magnetic field represented by the model's parameter. Through numerical simulations on a large-scale sample of randomly selected models, it was discovered that the model exhibits three distinct outcomes: the absorbing state with no external influence, the polarization in response to strong external magnetic fields, and an intermediate state with moderate fields. Analyzing the scaling of the interval of the intermediate phase, it was shown that this model exhibits a distinct type of dynamic critical phenomenon, with characteristics related to viscosities, and how magnetization decays over time.

The spread of respiratory viruses, transmitted through the air, is significantly influenced by atmospheric conditions. Understanding how these viruses behave and persist in different weather conditions is crucial for developing effective containment strategies. To tackle this challenge, a new mathematical model has been created to simulate the three-dimensional movement of virus-carrying particles in relation to air currents caused by a descending object. This novel model builds upon existing research, addressing a gap in studies that considered viral transmission models relative to descending objects. The underlying mechanisms of virus propagation were analyzed using an existing physical model, and various scenarios, such as sneezing, coughing and speaking, were simulated across different environmental conditions, taking into account factors like temperature, humidity, and the number of evaporating droplets over time. The results indicate that smaller droplets tend to stay suspended in the air longer, especially in cooler and more humid conditions, thereby increasing the potential for virus transmission. Furthermore, simulations of aerosol dispersion were conducted to visualize the movement of droplets, and the findings highlight the critical role of understanding and addressing the spread of viruses in different weather conditions.

The rising interest in applying machine learning to scientific problem-solving comes with a caveat: many machine learning models, particularly complex ones like deep neural networks, are shrouded in ambiguity. Although various studies have examined the issue of interpretability for specific machine learning models, there's a significant gap in our understanding of ambiguity for simple models when integrated into larger, more dynamic systems common in scientific applications. Current techniques for assessing machine learning model interpretability generally focus on static analyses, such as calculating the influence of individual inputs on outputs, but they fall short in considering how models behave under changing conditions. This limitation hinders our ability to fully comprehend the reliability of machine learning models in real-world scenarios. To bridge this understanding, we propose a comprehensive framework for evaluating ambiguity that encompasses (1) simple machine learning models, (2) condition-dependent contexts, and (3) dynamic systems. Furthermore, we suggest that any effective measure of ambiguity must meet five essential criteria and provide a initial set of 15 candidate measures of ambiguity across the proposed framework, along with their evaluation through simulations and case studies.

Given a weighted directed graph G, we establish a lower bound formula for its normality index. Additionally, we demonstrate that the edge ideal of a weighted tournament's normality index equals its symbolic power convergence index.

Using a large $N$ expansion, a discrete quantum matrix model is analyzed in detail,  
where the matrix sizes are fixed finite values. As the expansion proceeds, quantum  
corrections are equivalent to solving a matrix model whose numbers of matrices are  
odd multiples of $N$, ultimately providing a finite $N$ solution. Furthermore, it is  
demonstrated that the associated matrices can be derived from a set of classical ellipsoids  
through the application of uniformization maps, which are valid for all $N$.

Recent research into adaptive defense strategies for neural networks has revealed their limitations in real-world security contexts, mainly due to their susceptibility to simultaneous attacks and lack of adaptability to normal operational variations. To address these shortcomings, this study introduces a protective mechanism for neural network platforms, focusing on activation interval supervision as a fault-tolerance approach. We observe that excessive deviations from expected behavior in specific layers of these networks can indicate potential security threats. Consequently, we remove platforms with anomalous activity and adjust the network's learning process based on external feedback. A thorough evaluation of this method was conducted using normal and maliciously altered inputs targeted at multiple layers of the network. Results show that our approach achieves precise classification accuracy while effectively limiting the frequency of platform deviations. Additionally, we explored the potential to normalise platform activity distribution to minimize unnecessary platform removals.

The Romanian Ministry of Finance is currently utilizing a specialized algorithm 
within their information technology system to manage financial claims across multiple 
companies, where several businesses owe money both to the government and each other, 
and several entities receive money from the government but spend it on their goods 
and services, all within the same network, to determine the financial claims that 
need to be paid and the amounts due, to within a specified error margin, and within 
a reasonable time frame, from among the numerous possible combinations, to satisfy 
the given conditions, to the benefit of as many companies as possible, and to 
minimize the residual debt to the government, with significant results achieved 
with an algorithm created by the authors, whose fundamental features are explained 
here, along with its basic operations, in this paper, where its performance is 
evaluated through multiple test scenarios, and the algorithm is not limited to 
the application within the Romanian Ministry of Finance, as it can be adapted to 
settle debts in any similar commercial network, with two key advantages being its 
efficiency in terms of time, and its modular design, allowing the incorporation 
of additional business data, with the latter potentially enhancing the final outcomes, 
as shown by a logical formula, explicitly defined, and experimentally validated, 
to within statistical certainty, derived from the authors' earlier research, presented 
with clear outcomes, and the algorithm is presented within the framework of theoretical 
computer science, along with its underlying data structure

Building upon previous research, we have generalized the Jordanian twist to a family of twists that incorporate a specific set of derivations within the Lie algebra of the upper triangular $2\textrm{x}2$ matrix algebra. Furthermore, we have identified the specific conditions that must be met for this family of twisted coassociators to be considered consistent.

We tackle the challenge of building a shared semantic space across multiple languages without using labels or from a single large-scale dataset. In this work, we propose a novel, cluster-consistent representation approach for words that is based on the assumption that words forming a cluster should have a similar meaning within each language. Through this approach, we first identify multiple linguistic clusters by analyzing data from each language separately, and then employ a low-dimensional, consistent representation method to construct the shared semantic space. This method ensures that the encoded information about cluster structure is preserved during this process. Our experiments, conducted on seven datasets across three languages, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by accurately predicting clusters and translating words without the need for target language data. Notably, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches in this task.

The LHCb experiment at the LHC analyzed particle production from Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV, specifically measuring pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons with a statistical significance of 7.9 sigma. The collision data, collected during the running period, provided insights into particle rates and distribution patterns in transverse momentum and rapidity. After comparing the results to theoretical models, the analysis indicated that initial free-streaming particle behavior failed to fully explain the observations, particularly in the low-energy, low-$s_{\perp}$ regime of the protons, where interactions resembled those of a quark-gluon plasma.

Historically, annotated conversational datasets utilized to train models for Dialogue State Tracking (DST) have exhibited significant inaccuracies due to inherent labeling errors. Existing methods primarily focus on enhancing architectural design or integrating multi-source information to achieve improved performance, without addressing the inherent imperfections of these flaws. This study investigates the impact of label noise on DST and reveals that regardless of methodological sophistication, significant performance declines occur when faced with noisy labels. Moreover, it demonstrates that accurate annotation through active learning requires a relatively high-confidence prediction from models, thereby rendering many noisy labels useless. To mitigate this issue, a new framework called ASTI is proposed, which employs iterative data correction and active learning to significantly enhance the performance of models trained on conversational datasets containing erroneous labels.

In late October 2019, protests in Chile escalated to a violent and widespread demonstration, ultimately involving nearly 3 million people. To understand the underlying dynamics of this social phenomenon, a new mathematical model was developed to track the spread of participants over time and across the country's 14 regions. This model accounted for both individual decision-making processes and shifting demographic patterns, revealing a correlation between higher infection rates in northern regions and increased connectivity. Furthermore, an analysis of recent policy developments was conducted to observe their impact on the model's outcomes.

Researchers developed a novel, logical framework to determine how accurately star formation rates, calculated through spectral energy density analysis, reflect real conditions. To assess this accuracy, they evaluated the consistency between these estimated star formation rates and those derived from the brightness of infrared lines in stellar spectra. Focusing on the Tract 33 region in the Milky Way, they examined 30 clusters with less than $10^5\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ total mass. After filtering out the contribution from active galactic nuclei to the infrared lines' flux, they derived corrected flux values and star formation rates from the lines' spectra. Subsequently, they evaluated the relationship between these rates and those from spectral energy density analysis using a statistical tool known as a $\log N$-$\log N$ slope. The results indicated that for lower mass ranges, the estimates derived from spectral energy density analysis were accurate, with a slope close to 1, but for higher mass ranges, the estimates derived from spectral energy density analysis increased more rapidly than the actual star formation rates, with a $\log N$-$\log N$ slope of 1.5, indicating the need to adjust the theoretical relationships used in spectral energy density analysis to account for this discrepancy. In doing so, they discovered that one particular element, the extinction coefficient, played a crucial role in this adjustment and that adjusting it from its default value of 1.0 to 1.5 would resolve the issue.

We are studying the boundary of a cone defined by squared norms of biquadratics in two variables. This specific part of the boundary, where such polynomials have non-negative values, is distinct from the interior, characterized by polynomials that can be expressed as a sum of such squared norms. In a recent discovery by the first author and their colleagues, a method was presented for representing a specific segment of the boundary using sums of non-negative polynomials. This method involved decomposing the biquadratics into a sum of triquadratics in one variable. Given that it has been previously established that all non-negative polynomials can be expressed as such a sum when the degree is sufficiently high, it was also shown that the boundary between the SOS region and the interior of the cone is not a set of measure zero within the non-negative polynomials.

In the study of neutrino physics, non-unitarity in leptonic mixing matrices is forecast to produce measurable deviations in neutral current neutrino scattering during short baseline experiments._predictions_ of non-unitarity are influenced by neutrino mass ordering, which significantly impacts strategy. Utilizing open neutrino beam parameters that will be available from the FASER experiment at CERN, our analysis demonstrates that either neutrino mass ordering could serve as our primary focus. If the normal ordering holds, experiments combining FASER$\nu$ with LBL J-PARC beamlines offers our most viable pathway for detecting non-unitarity with a reachable threshold of $\mathcal{O}(1)$ GeV. In the event of inverted neutrino mass ordering, the necessary beam energy for such a detection rises to $\ge \mathcal{O}(100)$ GeV. These predictions are thoroughly illustrated for both scenarios.

Alphabet-based regular expressions with intersection and complement operations can effectively be utilized to represent and manipulate automata languages. This approach yields concise descriptions of transformations and filterings on automata, and studies of automata and regular languages often be best expressed with these enhanced regular expressions. Notably, settled questions regarding this topic have been explored through both theoretical automata and symbolic logic approaches, this paper presents a method through extended regular expressions that resolves the inclusion problem between these expressions. Additionally, the algorithm developed utilizes an effective normal form, which determines the smallest regular expression representing the difference between two extended regular expressions in IUCKNT-star format, and through this determination, the inclusion and equivalence relations are analyzed. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated to be sufficiently powerful for automata and general alphabets and its correct operation is meticulously verified through both co-inductive normal form proof and explicit construction of the regular expression difference.

This research employs a external memory focus module in an inertia-muscle-attracted virtual avatar navigation network to effectively manage and integrate relevant sensor data for accurate navigation. By utilizing this network, we were able to recover an agent's position and orientation with remarkable precision, even in complex environments filled with obstacles and virtual barriers. Experimental evaluations demonstrated the superior performance of our approach when compared to previous inertia-muscle-attracted virtual avatar navigation methods, with significant reductions in error rates. Furthermore, an open dataset has been made available for future studies on deep inertia-muscle-attracted virtual avatar navigation techniques.

We propose a novel type of three-dimensional Weyl semimetal called square-root elevated-order Weyl semimetal, and it corresponds to fractional Chern-number-valued nodal rings in 2D systems. This novel phase arises near the point where a semimetallic state and an insulator state border each other. We observe that the square-root fractional Weyl point is not robust and can be disrupted by nonmagnetic disorder, and we utilize the Landau level approach to demonstrate that the FNWP dissappears under a magnetic field.

This study presents a novel application of the quasi-reversibility (QR) method to address a data completion issue in the time-independent Maxwell's equations.  The researchers implemented the QR technique using finite elements and simulated the outcomes using SPECTRUM, a parallel direct solver. The results demonstrate that this approach effectively avoids the ill-posed nature of the problem while yielding stable and convergent solutions even in the presence of noise. The method's flexibility is further highlighted by its capability to incorporate various boundary conditions and mathematical models generalised from previous work. The study also encompasses three distinct test scenarios, executed both analytically and numerically, including 2D and 3D applications. The findings indicate that the method produces satisfactory solutions for clean data as well as in data conditions with noise. The developed formulation is versatile and can be adapted to various problems by modifying a source code that utilizes the SPECTRUM library. The SPECTRUM package provides excellent performance, boasting up to ten times better efficiency than traditional finite difference methods for 3D problems. The method's efficiency is further demonstrated by the ability to solve large-scale data completion problems, as evidenced by a test case involving a volume of 100 cubic meters.

This work introduces a parafermion vertex operator algebra associated with the Kac-Moody Lie algebra $osp(1|2n)$ at a specific level $k$. We establish its structure by determining its primary fields, descent constructs, and spiral elements, ultimately revealing its nuclear relationship with the Kac-Moody algebra $osp(1|2n)$ at levels $2k+n-2$ and $2k+n$.

Current Federated Learning methods generally allow only structurally compatible models to be combined, limiting their applicability when models have different architectures or when large numbers of models need to be integrated. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative approach called Federated Selective Integration (FSI) that enables a flexible and unified method to combine diverse models, regardless of their architecture. By leveraging diverse models, FSI leverages both shared understanding and unique aspects captured by each model. We introduce a flexible mechanism that allows models to contribute either globally unique information or model-specific data during the training process. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our method over baseline approaches, showing significant performance improvements and notable gains when integrating models on a large scale.

The entorhinal cortex of the mammalian brain is particularly significant due to its proximity to the hippocampus and correlated disease patterns.  Research into grid cells within the entorhinal cortex has primarily been conducted using invasive neuroimaging techniques on the rat brain.  To better comprehend the formation of grid cells, the availability of a comprehensive, publicly accessible dataset would facilitate extensive, invasive research without the need for duplicative experiments.  This study introduces a comprehensive dataset consisting of 215 recorded single-cell time series from the entorhinal cortex during a spatial navigation task.  To explore the dataset's key features, various analytical methods were performed, examining cell-spatial relationship metrics, spectral entropy, and visualization techniques.  Additionally, to demonstrate the data's rich information content, multiple clustering algorithms were assessed, alongside an exploration of data subset characteristics.

Solar differential rotation significantly contributes to the generation of the Global Solar Dynamo by concentrating the Turbulent Magnetic Field at the equator due to its rotation shear. This process is crucial in converting the Regenerative Magnetic Field into the Global one. Our study employs a robust statistical method using machine learning to analyze a sophisticated 3D magnetic fluid simulation that incorporates the effects of rotation and magnetic field interactions. By using a support vector regression tool, we established relationships between various turbulent magnetic field characteristics and the surrounding turbulent environment. Notably, we discovered that differences in differential rotation can lead to changes in both the amplitude and stability of cyclical magnetic phenomena. Specifically, we observed that rapid rotators exhibit more complex cycles associated with higher orders of chaotic behavior, while slower rotators experience simpler cycles. This phenomenon holds implications for potential magnetic cycles observed in太阳-like stars.

This paper examines the rank growth of elliptic curves over quartic fields belonging to the symmetric groups $S_4$ and $A_4$, specifically within quartic extensions of the rational numbers. While previous research has extensively covered $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic fields, focus on rank expansion has been limited to cases involving quadratic or cubic fields. We demonstrate the occurrence of rank expansion for an elliptic curve over $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic fields, based on 4-ratios of their 2-torsion subgroups over the rational numbers. Additionally, we investigate the set of elliptic curves with rank growth over $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic fields, derived from pairs of quartic fields with 2-ratios of their 2-torsion subgroups. Using computational methods, we identify over 30,000 such pairs of quartic fields, with more than 3,000 having 2-ratios of their 2-torsion subgroups over the rational numbers, enabling us to demonstrate the rank expansion of an elliptic curve over $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic fields.

Our study investigates quantum thermal equilibrium using time-dependent gravitational models that simulate thermal states and thermalizations. We examine how quantum thermal equilibrium and non-equilibrium states relate to each other through quantum field theory and gravitational duals, finding connections with quantum endothermy/exothermy, the Unruh temperature, and the nonlinear response theorem. Furthermore, we compare quantum thermal equilibrium to non-equilibrium states under quantum field theory and gravitational descriptions. Our analysis specifically focuses on quantum thermal states with negative QNEC for both smooth and discrete spectra cases. These findings are supported by quantum field theory, numerical simulations, and gravitational duals. Additionally, we derive a quantum thermal equivalence inequality for the Unruh temperature based on quantum thermal relaxations and equate it with a new gravitational equivalence. Our results show that the quantum thermal equivalence holds for SYK models, quantum harmonic oscillators, and their holographic duals, as well as quantum systems with discrete spectra cases, implying quantum thermal states with high entropies are similar to non-equilibrium states.

Quantum states evolve over time within a d-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and the fastest time this takes can be found using various types of quantum speed limits (QSL). In this study, we focus on identifying times for certain collapse and revival dynamics of a d-dimensional Bloch ball under unitary evolution, as well as deriving monotones applicable to these cases. We also explore how one of these, the asymmetry monotone, relates to quantum rate constraints and the time it takes for certain dynamics to occur within a certain range of dimensions. However, finding the exact time it takes for collapse and revival dynamics to repeat for all dimensions is an unresolved challenge.

The paper establishes a specific inequality for the norm of an interpolation operator related to the second difference of a function in the $L^1$-norm. 
This inequality is derived from a previously proven result. 
Furthermore, the author obtains a particular bound for the norm of the interpolation operator in the $L^p$-norm, where $1\le p\le \infty$, and demonstrates that a certain method of linear interpolation is optimal for $p=1$.

Microwave and terahertz frequencies span important regions of the electromagnetic spectrum that currently lack effective, non-destructive imaging methods using wavelengths in this range. By utilizing nanoscopy with terahertz light, we have created an imaging technique capable of visualizing the structure and electrical properties hidden beneath opaque materials at these frequencies. In this study, we apply our method to map a planar microwave resonator at 58 GHz, an obstacle that can't be imaged with higher frequency terahertz light. In order to do so, we near-field probe the sample with a metallic scanning probe gradually brought into resonance with the microwaves. As we do this, it picks up strong coupling between adjacent points of the microwave pattern, validating our method's accuracy when compared to conventional imaging techniques.

We introduce a new variant of equivariant motivic spectrum theory, incorporating a smooth, one-parameter family of algebraic curves within a surface. This new framework builds upon the existing equivariant motivic spectrum theory that considers a fixed curve as a group-equivariant extension over the function field of that curve. Within our new setup, the algebraic curves become modules in a way that facilitates the creation of mapping cones and universal coefficients isomorphisms, an important new property. These developments permit a deeper understanding and classification of the algebraic K-theory of those curves, becoming closely related to the K-theory of the underlying surface. This theory also establishes an equivalence between the K-theory of the curve and a combination of its Mumford-Tatemer isomorphisms and Milnor K-theory. Furthermore, we show that these results become relevant when studying how the algebraic K-theory varies in ways that align with expectations from conjectures regarding descent.

The development of a Venus-like atmosphere is an efficient process, one that rapidly occurs within short timeframes, potentially as quick as 10^7 years, to 10^8 years, regardless of initial water and volatile concentrations in the planet's mantle and crust. This rapid development arises from the established water vapor-sulfur dioxide-temperature feedback system and is further accelerated by a water vapor-radiation-carbon dioxide feedback as the atmosphere becomes more opaque. As a result, any planet lacking a protective magnetic field, located in the habitable zone boundary near stars like Sun, will quickly become a barren world resembling Venus, hindering the existence of liquid water within the planet's crust. Consequently, the location of a planet within its star's habitable zone alone is insufficient; rather, introducing water to an existing Venus-like atmosphere from external sources, such as meteorites comets, may result in a rich, water vaporized atmosphere containing sulfur dioxide, beneficial for sustaining water within a planet's crust and maintaining temperatures conducive to liquid water. This water-via-metals regulation system operates by creating an optimal balance between atmospheric escape and internalization of water, associated with the concentration of U.S. in the planet.

Investigating ultrafast and sub-atomic phenomena within molecular systems is
challenging, particularly when it comes to assessing instantaneous electrostatic
changes resulting from fast ionization. Researchers have previously used electrons
to ionize small organic molecules and glycol droplets, but this method presents
several limitations, including insufficient energy and difficult control of
interactions between electrons and molecules/droplets, which restricts the range
of observable phenomena. In contrast, utilizing photons offers several advantages
for studying electron dynamics, as it enables researchers to probe any material
and independently control interactions between light and matter. We present a novel
approach, referred to as reaction nanoscopy, that leverages the photoionization of
small glycol droplets to demonstrate its effectiveness. This method allows us to
observe internal hydrogen bonds in water mixed with alcohol, an example of an
超临界现象, and provides insights into their ionization. Through this method, we
have discovered that hydrogen bonds remain largely intact even after rapid
ionization, and that electrons and protons recombine to form a charge-separated
glycol state, which has significant implications for enhancing organic
photovoltaics and water-based electrolytes.

Mapping a many-body state to a matrix product state (MPS) provides an efficient representation, yet not all states can be represented this way. We discover that the set of MPS states corresponds precisely to those states which, when expressed as a circuit, maintain a constant depth when sliced vertically. Furthermore, we find that any state within this specific circuit category can be transformed into both an MPS state and a constant-depth unitary circuit with single-gate operations matching the original state's requirements. These findings are significant for both fundamental quantum information theory and practical applications in quantum simulation and computation, particularly in terms of swap-network constructions, hybrid classical-quantum algorithms, and the development of new computational models.

We introduce a hierarchical graph representation for digital pathology images,
utilizing an NDCardia network that extracts relevant features and categorizes them
from the cell to the tissue level. Our method incorporates NDCardia's output into
a downstream task through a hierarchical structure, reflecting the organization
of the pathology sample. The NDCardia network represents a comprehensive way to
decode the biological hierarchy within histology samples, providing a detailed
graph representation of extracted nuclei, along with their features and surrounding
environment. The hierarchical architecture of our network includes a bottom-up
branch for effective feature extraction of nuclei and a top-down branch for
interpreting the histology sample's organization. The proposed method can be
enhanced with prior knowledge from the Weber-Fechner law to improve feature
extraction and employ the Mixture of Professions framework to utilize different
nuclei expertise among virtual residents. The effectiveness of our approach is
validated by experimental results on the Pathology Length Estimation (PLE) dataset,
where NDCardia outperformed state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior
performance with only 1/40 of the parameters and 1/10 of the training time when
compared to a fully connected (FC) counterpart.

In various fields like finance, healthcare, and social networking, point process models are commonly used to analyze event data. For initial examinations of these processes, the non-linear Hawkes model is a popular choice. However, estimating its parameters has been challenging due to the lack of closed-form estimators. A new approach presented here provides a method for sampling from the non-linear Hawkes parameters' posterior distribution, incorporating BP-allocated probabilities into the likelihood calculation. This method is demonstrated with real-world Twitter dataset analysis, resulting in a outcome where an upward adjustment in hate speech within a political tweet dataset increases the estimated probability of future events by 14 to 19 cents within a 95% confidence level.

One significant challenge associated with calculating radiative transfer for application to astronomical bodies is the intricate nature of their surface geometry. A sophisticated technique known as the Rapid Multipole Expansion, has been developed to simplify this complex geometry by approximating it in multiple modes. In order to apply this technique effectively across various frequencies, a specific constraint must be met relative to the size of various geometric components. However, there is often a discrepancy between this limit and the moderate values typically used. We demonstrate that a particular form of this multipole model preserves angular momentum, which enables its safe use beyond this theoretical limit. This development is crucial in allowing the rapid application of 3D time-dependent radiative transfer simulations.

One major challenge in training automatic segmentation models is the lack of labeled training data for every target organ. Researchers have been successfully using Domain Adaptive Learning (DAL) to transfer pre-trained models to target domains. Nevertheless, DAL techniques still face limitations, such as requiring significant variations between source and target domains, and struggle with fine-grained adjustments within the same domain.

To address these issues, we propose Contrastive DAL (CADAL), a novel approach that integrates Contrastive Learning into the Domain Adaptive Learning framework for segmenting comparable anatomical structures. Initially, we enhance a Pre-trained model and source domain by introducing Contrastive Loss, a technique that encourages encoding similar data points closer together. Subsequently, we employ Fine-tuning to adapt the model to target domain, and DAL to encode target domain samples with the same encoding length as source domain samples, and apply an optimal translation to minimize the distance between the two encodings.

Our experiments on cardiac segmentation with the MMWHS dataset and liver segmentation with the LiTS and Spleen19 datasets demonstrate the superiority of CADAL over state-of-the-art methods, improving the Dice Similarity Coefficient by up to 5.11%, 1.04%, and 1.24% respectively. The CADAL framework's effectiveness for segmenting comparable anatomical structures is also demonstrated through ablation studies and additional results. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengx12/CADAL.

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively applied in the formulation of the BRS transformation for various multispinor supergravity theories. The standard approach to derive the BRS transformation for these theories is based on this '1.5 order trick'. The aim of this study is to demonstrate the inadequacy of the 1.5 order formalism in generating a consistent BRS transformation for the old minimal type supergravity, by relying on a straightforward argument, and consequently, existing derivations for other theories are likely to be flawed as well.

The interaction between high-intensity laser pulses and plasmas as a function of polarization has significant interest due to its varying outcomes under different polarization states. Despite previous experiments with low-intensity laser pulses, investigating this effect in high-intensity regimes has been largely unexplored. In this study, we compare the interaction outcomes for circularly polarized and linearly polarized multi-petawatt laser pulses with under-dense plasma and investigate how polarization alteration influences the results. With the 1.05$\mu$m laser, we observe a notable increase in electron intensity up to an order of magnitude when switching from linear to circular polarization, primarily caused by the extended interaction length associated with the latter. At shorter wavelengths of 0.80$\mu$m and 0.526$\mu$m, we instead see a notable increase in electron energy by two to three orders of magnitude with circular polarization, predominantly caused by the increased acceleration length resulting from resonance shifts due to polarization alteration and not interaction length. In all cases, we instead observe notable enhancements in the proton energy with circular polarization when using the 1.05$\mu$m laser, and simultaneously, both effects contribute to the resonance shift and resonant absorption enhancement with circular polarization when employing shorter wavelength lasers.

Using updated data on the $e^+e^-\to \tau^+\tau^-$ process at center-of-mass energies below 2$s$, we place more stringent constraints on the effective contact interactions of the $\tau$ lepton. Consequently, our refined limits on the $\tau$ lepton's dipole form factors are significantly improved, particularly for the $g_a^e$ and $g_a^\tau$ couplings.

This paper addresses the challenge of decoding rank metric errors under an asymmetric deployment. We introduce a new asymmetric rank metric and establish a correlation between asymmetric and symmetric rank metric mistakes. Building on this relationship, we propose a method to correct asymmetric rank metric mistakes, which also functions correctly with symmetric mistakes. The performance of our scheme has been verified through simulations.

In the context of AdS/CFT, extended operators within a conformal field theory are researchers' focus, particularly those carrying spin under a AdS group. The general characteristics of these operators are still largely unknown save for correlation function insights. The primary objective of this paper is to provide crucial insights into the AdS W-primary operators' operator product expansion, specifically the spin-2 case, under the assumption that these operators exist within certain AdS super-CFTs. The authors derive novel constraints on the spin and representation of descendent operators generated when an AdS W-primary is combined with a super-CFT primary with high spin. The case of the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ model is explored in detail, incorporating additional constraints from crossing symmetry on the resulting equations from such four-point correlation functions. The resulting implications on the AdS$_3$ sector's spectrum are generated and analyzed. The authors further derive the complete spectrum within a specific subset of the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ superblock containing spin-2 AdS W-primary operators. The connection to the generalized unitarity approach for constructing AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ superblocks is discussed as well.

A significant hurdle in current research is accurately measuring the correlation of large-scale structures from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) polarisation power spectrum. Researchers are utilizing deep-learning methods to reduce this correlation's impact by first predicting the gravitational wave patterns obscured by Neutrino streams. We demonstrate an effective approach by training a neural network to simultaneously remove the effects of neutrino gravity waves and large-scale structural distortion. By utilizing simulations of a non-Gaussian primordial tensor disturbance, we find that our approach successfully separates the two influences. Furthermore, when applying this technique to actual data, our neural network model reduces residual distortion patterns to a more precise level, surpassing the level achieved by traditional methods.

The paper provides the underlying vector space structure for the algebraic definition of Pontrjagin classes by Gelfand and MacPherson. Furthermore, it supplies a corresponding manifold interpretation for this definition. The author demonstrates the equivalence between this and the classical topological approach to defining these classes. A particularly straightforward ground for examining the relationship among these various definitions is the orthogonal group.

We investigated SN 2020jfo, a Type II-S supernova with an unusually short plateau duration, using both optical and near-infrared observations. The onset of the H$\alpha$ emission seen in optical spectra and the start of the plateau in infrared light curves occurred at nearly the same time. Analysis of the spectral features and the shape of the break in the color evolution suggest that SN 2020jfo is likely associated with a low-velocity, hydrogen-rich ejecta. A detailed study of the supernova's light curves, particularly during the early phases, was performed using the "Two Component Model" (TCM). This model indicated that SN 2020jfo's luminosity during the plateau phase (around $1.4 \times 10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$) and its color temperature (approximately $9000$ K) during the plateau descent were typical of Type II supernovae. The TCM analysis also provided an estimate of the supernova's distance, which was found to be $180 \pm 10$ Mpc, consistent with host galaxy measurements.

We analyze striped lobster-eye lens arrays for X-ray imaging, explaining their operation in detail and addressing issues like blurred images within specific angular ranges. The performance of these lenses has significantly improved in recent years, making them excellent candidates for precise Stripped-LoBster-Eye-X-Ray-Optics(StripeLEXX) images over a wide range of angles. 180°. The stripe-lectroscope concept can also offer enhanced features, such as increased sensitivity and lower energy requirements, compared to traditional lobster-eye lenses. To demonstrate their effectiveness, we evaluate this concept for detecting supernovae and other transients across the sky, specifically using the Wide-Field Survey Telescope on the Fermi Gamma-Ray Satellite as a model. By detecting gamma-rays over a wide field of view, the stripe-lectroscope would allow for accurate localization of X-ray events within a few degrees, thus filling the gap between the current energy ranges. The stripe-lectroscope shows comparable or better sensitivity to hard X-ray burst triggers than the Fermi trigger, and requires roughly three times fewer detectors than the WF-SPI on the Integral satellite for the same performance, or can detect bursts softer in energy.

We've established a stage-set version of partial uniform ellipticity and the Bogdanovskii-de Giorgi-Nash theorem under uniform growth conditions, and this is followed by a second theorem with exponent bounds and partial Hölder continuity conclusions.

Recent research has emphasized the significance of the velocity field function in
understanding galaxy and group dynamics within the $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model.
To further explore this area, a study introduces a 2D halo weight function in the
velocity field to investigate its theoretical and observational implications.
By leveraging spectral sequence models and simulation data, researchers utilize
spectral networks to predict the halo weight function and evaluate its sensitivity
to fundamental parameters of the $\Lambda$CDM model. The predictive accuracy of
this IA reaches remarkable levels of sensitivity, with some parameters being
predicted with a relative error under 1$^{-5}$, indicating the field's high
sensitivity to these parameters. Additionally, a study compares the effectiveness
of this approach with random forest models, demonstrating the spectral network's
superior performance. The researchers also investigate the velocity field function's
capacity to distinguish between different dark matter models, as well as the
feasibility of applying this approach to observational data to differentiate the
properties of these models.

AiNMF proposes a novel Semi-Supervised Convolutive Non-negative Matrix Factorization method for music sheet transcription from audio. This technique utilizes convolutive NMF and pre-defined peak detection points to locate onsets, combined with a technique called Warping by Example to warp the basis spectra into a sequence matching the corresponding onsets. This method is particularly effective when applied to a small set of input scores to extract both temporal and frequency features from the audio. AiNMF achieves superior results, surpassing current SOTA standards on both general and challenging evaluation sets of the MIDI-to-Music Score task at the recent Challenge on Musical Score Synthesis and Transcription at ISMIR 2019. To participate in this challenge, a Python library has been released on GitHub.

A new, comprehensive approach is presented for computing rotating stars in the context of general relativity. This method develops solutions incrementally from slowly to rapidly spinning stars through iterative, non-linear calculations. By demonstrating the approach with multiple examples and showing its consistency with known results for non-rotating stars and limiting cases of fluid fluids rotating as irrotational flows, a potential pathway is established for comparing the outcomes with neutron star observations.

A major challenge in creating models that can automatically process and categorize complex documents is finding a model architecture that can handle the visual information contained within, without requiring a model to learn from labeled examples of simple, basic document templates.
Previous models achieved this by learning from labels that indicated category names or by leveraging segmentation labels that identified specific document elements.
This work presents a novel approach that uses an unconstrained training setting, in which models are trained without segmentation, labels or any pre-defined document templates.
Instead, it proposes using a unique document encoding framework that can efficiently encode simple documents and design an attention-based model decodder that can accurately decode model predictions based on this efficient encoding.
This unconstrained training setting is demonstrated to be highly effective, requiring 10 times fewer training samples and yet reaching 95% of the performance of leading models that require labels indicating document elements.
Additionally, it requires only 70 times fewer samples and reaches 75% of the performance of leading models that use unary documents.
Therefore, it significantly reduces the expensive data-labeling required for segmentation for visually simple documents.

Researchers have investigated using deep learning techniques to detect and classify the signal characteristics of gravitational waves resulting from neutron star-black hole mergers. Although prior studies have demonstrated success with deep learning models for detecting these events, their performance in identifying the properties of the merging objects was not as effective. We observed a significant improvement in classification accuracy after optimizing the input data, which led to a classification accuracy of 99.18% at a confidence level of 5 sigma. Our deep learning models also achieved the best performance in distinguishing neutron star-black hole mergers from other types of compact binary coalescences. Furthermore, we were able to clear a background noise test with a noise confusion measure of 6.7 standard deviations, which indicates our models can reliably distinguish these signals from background noise. Additionally, our models achieved remarkable results in recovering the masses of the merging objects, outperforming existing methods in certain mass ranges. We also propose a novel deep learning classifier that considers both signal and noise components. This multi-channel model achieved a mass recovery accuracy of 0.24 solar masses when testing a broad mass range, which is comparable to the performance of the conventional matched filtering method. Our findings are detailed through multiple sets of figures illustrating model performance in various aspects.

This paper introduces the Marker-driven Neural Network (MarkNeural) framework, a framework that utilizes the marker-driven approach to automatically design neural networks using data. The purpose of using machine learning in the context of social wellness is to identify the key factors that influence social wellness by analyzing determinants of social determinants. The goal of the MarkNeural framework in this specific application is to establish connections between social determinants and social wellness, while also providing a means to explore social wellness in terms of its underlying determinants. The MarkNeural framework combines elements of the marker-driven design approach with multi-objective optimization to create a set of high-performance, marker-based neural networks called Objective-Recursive-Generative Networks (ObjGenNets). The resulting framework successfully extracted the key features of social determinants from a dataset consisting of U.S. counties, and demonstrated remarkable performance through comparative analysis. The mark深度学习 framework is expected to have a positive impact on both social wellness and the field of machine learning.

This paper builds upon the work of  Le (2019), which determined an optimal periodic
  movement for a viscous "scallop" within a Hele-Shaw layer.  Given that the
  periodic movement of the scallop is now fixed, this study seeks to find the
  best shape that would generate a specific periodic movement with the least
  drag force.  We consider two scenarios: a) the scallop has a fixed shape but
    we are looking for the ideal movement, and b) the ideal shape is being sought
    regardless of the movement.  We examine multiple applications, including
   within mucus layers, coral polyps, and micro-pumps.

Our analysis of mobile data during the COVID-19 pandemic in four U.S. urban areas reveals significant changes in urban social economic patterns.  Unlike previous studies using aggregate metrics, our research examines social economic patterns across different income groups through the lens of entropy.  We discover that while the pandemic initially diminished overall entropy, it also amplified entropy differences between lower and higher income regions, particularly in Chicago and Chicago.  Further investigation into human mobility behavior using maximum entropy modeling indicates that people from lower income brackets reduced their daily entropy by up to 50% in Chicago and Chicago, compared to less than a 20 reduction in lower income regions.  In contrast, residents from higher income brackets maintained similar entropy differences as pre-pandemic levels.  Our findings suggest that mobility restrictions during the pandemic had varying effects on different income groups in urban settings and may contribute to the widening gap in urban inequality.  The magnitude of this contribution is substantial in cities like New York and Chicago.

Observations of young stellar objects suggest they grow by accreting mass and merging with other mass-accreting systems, and a new model of massive star formation reflects this by allowing the accretion process to involve both disordered mass fluctuations and the merging of multiple clumps over time. This statistical approach to the process was applied to a hypothetical system like W51-Ω25, evaluating the effects of outbursts and mergers on a set of outer boundaries and internal structures, as well as on the temperature and spectral characteristics of the system. Comparisons with real-world observations revealed that the model's predictions for mass fluctuations, the age of the system's structure, and its temperature all matched well with actual data, suggesting that a stochastic approach to the accretion process is a crucial component of developing more comprehensive models of massive star formation.

For a massive wedge-shaped system in two dimensions, we employ endomorphisms defined by the Chiral CFT-LICFT boundary conformal field theory to generate a network of observables. For massless theories, this approach fails due to the presence of unitary boundaries. We then examine superselection sectors within this network and observe that its structure is closely related to that of a module over a chiral network, with a key distinction being the presence of infinitely many non-isomorphic, irreducible sectors.

The controversy surrounding 5G technology's safety has sparked our interest in exploring the radiation from 5G towers that is emitted over vulnerable populations, including children and medical facilities. To accomplish this, we developed a method for identifying children, schools, hospitals, and other high-traffic areas near cellular towers in the United States, as well as mapped out children and hospitals in the United Kingdom. Our statistical approach provides a framework for examining how much radiation from 5G towers is emitted over these locations. Through this method, we discovered that nearly 66% of the American population is living within close proximity to a cellular tower within half a kilometer, yet only about 0.19% of American children are regularly exposed to 5G radiation. Similarly, nearly 6% of American schools are located within half a kilometer of a cellular tower. In the United Kingdom, approximately 4.5% of children are regularly exposed to 5G radiation. Through this methodological approach, we can easily examine how radiation from 5G towers is emitted over children, schools, hospitals, and other high-traffic areas.

We derive a Hamiltonian Dysthe approximation for three-dimensional gravity waves on a deep water surface with constant vorticity, undergoing the weak nonlinearity interaction of two plane wave trains moving in perpendicular directions. When analyzed at a critical resonance, this model simplifies to a Dysthe equation with constant vorticity, whose solution undergoes near-perfect conservative modulation,不受 1D Euler-Cortewall soliton non-conservation的影响. Furthermore, this approach provides insights into the structure of the Dysthe equation with constant vorticity, particularly in regions where large vorticity leads to substantial energy redistribution within a localized region.

We have developed a differential structure for locally convex functions that is robust against convergence, and have demonstrated its suitability for the study of geometric differential forms through the example of Stokes' Theorem. Moreover, we have provided a proof of the Stokes Theorem within this differential context.

Autonomous vehicles navigate using a navigation manager that fuses sensor inputs for optimal performance in dynamic environments. This system is designed to manage layers of navigation, with each layer powered by a different sensor blending immediately with a vote-based decision process. The concept of immediately sonar blending is demonstrated through a 2D simulation, where the sonar data is used to create a global map, adjust the vehicle's speed, and guide it around obstacles. The sonar-based path planning is supplemented by other sensors, with a decision process determined by a weighted vote system. The result is a robust and adaptable navigation system capable of efficient obstacle avoidance and quick integration of additional sensors.

The proliferation of fake news on social media poses a significant threat,
especially when it appears in various formats and languages. Detecting
fraudulent news has become an urgent challenge across multiple domains, and
the rise of multimedia posting on social media exacerbates this challenge.
To tackle this issue, researchers have explored several approaches, including
using pre-trained classifiers and leveraging entity linking technology to
enhance accuracy. However, less attention has been devoted to employing
summarization techniques to assist in detecting fake news. This research utilizes
abstractive summarization to enhance the detection accuracy of news with
associated entities and without them. It demonstrates that using summarization
techniques aids in identifying fake news, regardless of entity information, and
further demonstrates its effectiveness with entity-linked entities and additional
analysis of summary characteristics through visualization techniques.

This research investigates a new phenomenon known as the bending influence in high-dimensional random fields, specifically within the context of the 2-eigenfunction of a Gaussian field. We establish that as the dimension increases, this phenomenon becomes dominant, ultimately determining the asymptotic behavior of the 2-eigenfunction. Furthermore, we analyze the interplay between various competing factors in Gaussian spaces and provide insights into the general mechanisms at work. Our study also extends to certain smooth function cases and relates to gravitational wave detection.
